title: Best Bang For Your Buck
text:
Of all of the headphones I've used to date, I've found that these ones definitely offer the most "bang for your buck!" I highly recommend them. In fact, I can't recommend them enough. I'm on my third pair, and I've consistently experienced the same quality from each.

Here are the short, sweet points:

1) Ninety percent of the time, I use mine for running and biking with my iPhone/iPod. I sweat obnoxiously, and they still hold up against the "moisture" (which is an understatement). They're definitely durable. If you're that athlete hunting for "the pair", these are a solid bet to go with!

2) They really don't kid about the "ultra lightweight" aspect! These are amazingly lightweight and flexible, and that lends to an amazing fit. They don't hurt my ears (or head) from pushing or squeezing too firmly.

3) The sound quality is great for my standards. These compare (or surpass) any I've used.

4) The only (minor) issue I experience is that if they ever come out of my ears for a moment (i.e. I bump them or take them out to say "hey" to someone), sweat can get into my ear, and they sometimes run into issues. It's rare, and the results are typically minor, but it can create that "underwater" effect, reducing the volume and quality slightly. Usually, a simple re-shift or drying out of my ear will alleviate the problem.

5) If was being really picky, I'd say they could also benefit from a cord management system (e.g. a free clip). However, relative to others, they have a pretty ideal cord length (i.e. as little excess as seems possible).

If you've read this far and want my typical "wordier" review, read on for my follow-up points:

1) Sweat/Life: Like anything, they're not invincible. They don't even claim to be waterproof, so more power to them! Typically after five to six months of using each pair daily, they eventually bite the dust. That's from one to two hour workouts, constantly being chucked in and out of a gym bag, and surviving whatever other wears come their way. Toward the end of their life, I'll eventually begin to experience an occasional short-out in one of the speakers during the "peak" of my workout (a.ka. the part where I sweat nastiest). However, they'll dry out by the next day and be good to go. After about another month of this routine, they'll become unusable. From my experience, that's a great lifespan- especially for the price you can find these at.

2) Fit: They sit so gently set in my ear canals, yet they stay in so well. I've never had them come off unless I accidentally knock them off. Honestly, I've sort of "forgotten" I have them in at times. Because I don't think about them, I've gone to scratch my head or wipe sweat, and I've dumbly knocked them lose. They're design blows my mind. It's just so ideal. I've even gone through a number of hair-dos (ranging from longer to completely buzzed), and they still stay on just as well. They're very adjustable because of a precise range of ratcheted positions.

3) Sound Quality: I can't say I've owned "premium sound" sound sport headphones, so this is always the toughest part for me to review. I like to think that I know good sound and appreciate high quality. Based on that alone, I say these are great. I pump songs with heavy bass (i.e. budstep, rock, etc...), and they sound great to me. More "objectively", I can at least compare them to other things like my premium car audio, Apple Earbuds, and so forth. Based on all of that, they sound just as good to me.

4) Sweat (Part 2): I don't have much extra to say here. Basically, this is rarely an issue, but it's a point worth noting. Because they're not water proof, they don't have any special seals. I just make a habit of not taking them out until I'm done, and everything is usually fine. I just pause my music if I need to stop and hear something. And that's not to say I can't ever take them out. I've done so many times without any problem. It's just a rule I've made to avoid even risking it.

5) Cord Management: I rarely notice this problem. I generally just let them hang and don't run into issues. Because of they're great fit, I can easily throw the cord behind me or wear it down the front- depending on how I'm working out. On rare occasions, I use a clip from an old pair of headphones, and that helps a lot. Personally, I just hate dealing with clips, so it's almost not even worth the extra effort.

It might be important to note that I have used several various headphones over the years, and these are what I ended up on. To give you some comparison, I have tried various Apple "Earbuds" (i.e. [[ASIN:B004DEPOA0 Apple Earphones with Remote and Mic (NEWEST VERSION)[Retail Packaging]]]), Griffin TuneBuds (i.e. [[ASIN:B0015ADWMW Griffin TuneBuds Mobile for iPhone 3G, 3GS (Black)]]), and even nicer Sennheiser sport sets (i.e. [[ASIN:B001GT185K Sennheiser PMX80 In-Ear Sport Series II Behind the Head Earphones]]).

Also, the in-ear pads are made of a cheap flimsy plastic and pop out. The medium and large plastic pieces don't even come close to fitting inside. All in all, these are good earbuds for a very specific use. If you are frustrated by your headphones falling out of your ears while working out, these are for you. However, if you are looking for top notch sound quality, you should pass on these.

title: Skullcandy INK'D vs. JVC Marshmallow . . . which one comes out ahead?
text:
When it comes to in-ear, noise blocking type earphones, I had been using JVC Marshmallows for a couple of years, but since these Skullcandy INK'D earphones were less expensive, are extremely popular, and pretty highly rated, I decided to give them a try.

A major difference is that the Skull candy ear bud is made of pliable material (probably silicone rubber), while the Marshmallow buds are made of hard sponge. Skullcandy provides three different sizes of buds, so hopefully you will get a nice fit. The middle sized one fit me the best, and when inserted in the ear, I can very quickly and easily get a nice tight, sealed fit, that blocks most ambient noise. The sound quality is very good, for music, with good bass response, and room for the music to resonate. The earphones are also good for podcasts or audio books, where the midtones of voices sounds nice and full.

Noise blocking earphones, with earbuds that seal in the ear canal, usually have the 'stethoscope effect'. This involves the transmission of sound, through the wires, and into the ear. The sound is similar to tapping a live microphone, a muffled bumping sound, which can be very irritating. Sound is transmitted amazing well through the cable and the soft Skullcandy earbuds. So if you are doing something where you are moving around and bumping the cord, or have clothing rubbing against the cord, some annoying sounds will most likely be transmitted into the ear. A really strong wind can also transmit sound. This problem is not as pronounced with the JVC phones.

Long term, the hard sponge JVC buds will probably outlast the silicone ones on the INK'D's. In addition, JVC also provides a spare set of buds, so for durability, JVC comes out ahead. For comfort though, the Skullcandy phones might have the edge. They may not block out as much noise, and may transmit some unwanted sounds, but they seem lighter and don't need to be adjusted as much to get a good fit.

The earphones are in the same price range, and both provide good performance, come in a variety of colors, and have a straight pin jack, instead of an L shaped one, which is generally less prone to breakage. If you really want to block out ambient sound, the JVC does a better job. If you prefer a little more comfort, and can live with some possible noise, the Skullcandy may work well. For the INK'D earphones, typically at Amazon, there is usually one color that is cheaper than the others, so if you wait a while the color you prefer may eventually be the one that is on sale.

title: Adorable colors, smart design (plug slightly shorter?)
text:
The Moshi Moonrock lime color looks very adorable. This obviously doesn't affect the music quality, but it can make them good gift candidates. The headphones are stored in a see-through plastic container that looks like shrink-wrap frustration but you can easily open it with fingers and maybe nails. Two additional ear plug sizes are included (the medium size is installed on the earphones). Also included is a small user manual in many languages. The english part is two pages long. The font is fairly small.

There are three ways to figure out the left/right earphones: 1) the click button is on the right side, 2) the head of the right earphone matches the color scheme (lime in this case) while the head of the left earphone is white 3) a L and R is written next to the point where the audio cable connects to the headphone head.

The sound is as expected in this price range. You are not going to get audiophile quality under $50, but you are also getting better sound than basic headphones included with many devices or you find at the checkout stand in mass market stores.

There are three main areas to cover in this review.

1. Playing music with the 3.5mm cable
Most of the devices I used it with had no problems, but a couple did have problems. The Samsung Chromebook has a known issue with the way its headphone port is designed, so make sure you put the cable all the way in. Initially I didn't realize this, and I could only get audio from the right ear.

The other issue is with the good old Creative Lab Zen mp3 player. Putting the cable all the way in, does not produce good sound. If I leave the cable one step out of the headphone slot, the sound is normal. The Zen was fine with 3 different earphones and two different headphones I tried after noticing this.

This got me looking. An unscientific comparison showed the Moshi plug was very slightly shorter than the other five earphones and headphones.

The majority of devices have no problem. I tried a number of devices after noticing this problem and they had no issues, including the iPod 4 Touch, LG Nexus 4, two older Android phones, original Kindle Fire, Sandisk Clip and Clip Plus mp3 players. Before noticing the problem, I tried it with more devices, but I did not keep track of them since I wasn't expecting this type of an issue to crop up.

2. Click button works with some devices
The Moshi Moonrocks are advertised as Kindle Fire HD headphones, but the Click functionality works with other devices as well in varying degrees. The Play/Pause function works in more devices, but the Next/Previous work with fewer devices.

For example, on the LG Google Nexus 4, all works with the Google Music app. With the Amazon Cloud Player, the previous doesn't work. With the Rdio app, only Play/Pause works. With the YouTube app, play/pause works (I didn't try YouTube playlists, so I don't know if Next/Previous works).

On the iPod 4 Touch with the latest iOS version installed, all four functions work with the Amazon Cloud Player, but only 3 out of 4 with the Rdio app.

It did not work with: first generation Kindle Fire with the native Amazon Music app, Samsung Chromebook, Honeycomb hardware Acer Android tablet, older Android 2.x phone

3. Wrapping the cables
The contraption for wrapping the cables is actually a smart idea but it takes some getting used to it and practice. Once you figure it out, it's fairly easy to get them in and out. Granted, not as fast as throwing them in a bag :)

To put them in the headphone storage:
a. align the two cables attached to the earphone heads into the Y groove of the base
b. the bottom of the storage inverts downwards like a skirt and stays fairly put
c. with the bottom inverted, wrap the cables around it
d. lift up the bottom

To unwrap the headphones, invert the bottom, and unwrap the cables.

title: Good things (frequently) must come to an end
text: I've been using variations of this model of earbuds since I was at least 17. I'm almost 23 now. They went from being "bumpin buds" with multicolored silicone tips to the current incarnation. Admittedly, though, they looked exactly the same- just colors and marketing have changed. Safe to say, I've been through over 8 pairs of these headphones. My average was at least two per year. In the beginning, it was because of my cat chewing them, but later, because they didn't last long. The longest pair I had was my last one, which was an astonishing 10.5 months. In general, you can churn out about 6 months per pair if you use them every day like me. The issue is ALWAYS with the wire connecting to the bud- it always ends up wearing out inside the insulation and stops working on one side or the other, rendering the stereo experience difficult. Honestly, I just got used to and accepted the fact that headphones don't last long, but I've finally grown tired of it. Most people I know have different pairs from different brands that last them 3+ years. I always kept a spare pair of these Sony's in my drawer as I knew it was only a matter of time. Well, it's time to move on. I kept coming back to these because the sound quality blows everything else I've tried out of the water, including Skullcandies (my previous affiliation with the same durability issues). However, I'm officially breaking the streak and finally venturing out to find a new brand or model that beats these in both sound quality and durability. Take it from me- these were not designed to last, and Sony probably knows it. I have one more pair in my drawer. It will be the last one I own.

text:

I hooked these up to my phone super easy (it's nice you can pair with more than one device, which I hear was a limitation of the previous generation) and pop one in my ear. I then start a show on Netflix and am able to conk out. Having no wires coming from my phone is amazing - I have been using headphones to help me sleep for a while and this is so much more convenient.

Apparently these are sweat-proof as well, but I (fortunately) don't do that while sleeping so I can't speak about that.

Overall, I'm actually really happy I purchased these. The battery life is about 5 hours, which is about 4.75 hours longer than I actually use, so I could see others knocking it but for me it isn't a big deal.

title: Great Sound
text:
These have actually been the best bluetooth headphones I've tried. They've been staying in my ears extremely well. Once I played with the sizing a bit they were very comfortable. I thought the clear plastic ring bit was odd, but it does seem to help.

The battery life isn't gigantic, but there's only so much you can expect when you want to buy something this small. If you want a bigger battery, at this point you still need a bigger device.

I initially didn't like the controls being down on the cord, but after trying it a bit I realized that this kept me from scraping my nails on the part that's in my ear while trying to use them, which was always an unpleasant experience on that devices where that happened.

I typically am outside when using these, and for safety reasons in many parts of the neighborhood I prefer to have only one of them in my ear so that I can hear cars and such. For those times, I usually have a hat on and run the cord through/under the hat to the other side of my head and the hat keeps it so that I can have one- or even both - sides out of my ears without the whole thing flopping all over the place or falling off entirely.

Having them deliver feedback about the state of their battery over bluetooth to be displayed on devices like iPhones is a nice touch as well. In addition, there are audio prompts to alert you when they're turning on, turning off, trying to pair with something, and what the state of their battery is.

I would like more battery life, but I really can't hold that against them. Otherwise, these do just about everything that I think is remotely reasonable to ask for given the size and price constraints they had to work with. It's a really polished product that's worked well for me as I've experimented with an iPhone and several different Android tablets.

title: Top notch BT earbuds - if you are looking for a bluetooth solution for working out and you're a huge sweater, read this.
text:
Fantastic set of bluetooth earbuds, especially for working out. They have terrific sound, are very lightweight and have a lot of nice features. Be sure to try all three sets of eartips to make sure you get a good tight fit. This makes an enormous difference in bass response and with how well they keep out outside noise.

****Read if you sweat a lot around your head when you work out****
I sweat a lot when I work out...I mean a lot! I've killed three other sets of bluetooth earphones that claimed to be sweatproof. In all three cases, sweat leaked into the electronics and the buttons stopped responding. After a while, I couldn't turn them on anymore and they were junk. The Backbeat Go 2 also claims to be sweatproof but I actually believe their claims for the most part. The one thing that makes we wonder a bit is that there is a little rubber door on the top edge of the right earbud that comes open to reveal the mini-USB charge port. They made the door out of rubber and it seals but this still seems like a possible entry-point for sweat. However, this is easily fixable using Glad Press N Seal. Press N Seal is like Saran Wrap (clear plastic wrap you use to seal food containers) but is translucent, instead of clear and has kind of a sticky texture - no actual adhesive though. It wraps very tightly around things like tin foil. For these ear buds, I'd recommend getting some of this wrap, removing the eartips and stabilizers and wrapping a 1" by 2" piece around each earbud to cover up the cracks and USB door. (Obviously, don't cover up the port where the sound comes out into the eartip.) Then, replace the eartips and stabilizers and they are almost guaranteed to be sweatproof. If you wanted to be extra-safe, you could wrap the remote on the cord as well. Each time you plug it in to charge, you'll need to remove and reapply the wrap to the right side. I realized this is a pain but like I've said, I've gone through three headsets and am sick of paying for electronics that end up junk. If you sweat a lot around your head and you intend to use these for working out, I would recommend doing this.

title: Great headphones for a great price!
text:
I would NOT recommend these headphones for audiophiles. I'm sure they would pick it apart and have plenty of complaints. But as somebody who just wanted a pair of phones to listen to music on the commute to and from work, it works great! Deep bass, mids and highs are clear. I don't find it all that muddy, but I'm by no means an audiophile. I think the sound quality is superb for the price tag--you can't beat it. The microphone also works superbly--I use it to call people while on the train and people on the other end can hear everything the conductor announces.

The comfort level is also decent. As someone who occasionally wears glasses, the pressure does end up giving me a slight headache after 45 mins when pushing the frames into my temples. But when I wear contacts, no issues whatsoever. Comfortable to listen to music for at least a few hours (haven't tried beyond that). My ears don't get sweaty, the headband stays put, and the cord doesn't get tangled as I jam out on the train ride home.

The only downside I would say is that they're definitely not sound isolating. My boyfriend tells me that at a certain volume he can vaguely hear sounds, and then louder than that he can start to actually hear my music. So if you plan on blasting these at top volume, your neighbors might not appreciate it so much.

Overall, a great set of headphones that serve exactly the purpose that I wanted it to fulfill. Haven't had any interaction with the customer service yet, but have seen tons of raving reviews about them, so am confident that they will provide wonderful service should I need anything.

title: Surprisingly good sound .. When you take off comfort foam in ear cups :)
text:
I bought these late last year after reading some positive reviews, but even after burning in for over 40 hours per the manufacturer recommendation, I still found the sound quite muddy, flat, and just not clear.

I own several headphones - Fostex T50RP MK3, Sennheiser HD 558, Harman Kardon BT, Sony MDR-V6, Grado SR80e, and while I certainly don't expect headphones this cheap to measure up, I did expect something closer to Koss KSC75 performance, but it was far, far from that..

Over the last few months, I'd occasionally pull them out and have another listen to see if my ears or brain had adjusted to their sound... Nope...

UNTIL I pulled off the pleather covers on the ear cups, and removed the foam and VOILA, they were transformed from "ugh" to "not bad for $10!" Whereas before I literally couldn't use them ever because the sound was sooo bad to my ears, now I take them with me on short walks when I don't want to be afraid of a little sprinkle or dust or anything else taking them out but don't feeling like stuffing in-ear headphones into my ear canals...

Comfort definitely took a hit, but surprisingly, not as much as I'd have imagined - and for a short walk of an hour or less, I didn't find them uncomfortable without the pads.

Short story: love the color, simple design, single cable on right cup only, control on cord for pausing / playing, advancing to next or going back a track, and the sound is now enjoyable and very satisfactory at this price point.

text:
I've been using the first set of Klipsch S4 earphones for years without problem. I saw the white version of the S4-II at half the price of my original S4's and decided to get these as a backup pair. For this price nothing can beat the quality of these gems. The comments others have made about the cord moving being audible when moving around don't happen to mine at all. They sound crisp and clear with a full balanced tone even when I move around a lot.
I think one very important factor that many are unaware of is that these earphones need a break in period just as the original S4's did. This break in will "season" the sound of these tiny speakers. You will notice a world of difference in sound quality if you will just do the following:
Plug in your earphones to a good CD player and adjust the volume to about half the sound level you listen to at the highest volume you prefer, say my loudest volume would be 18 on my portable CD player so I set the volume to 9 and let them play for about 40 hours at this level. This break in period is essential and as I said you'll notice a world of difference after you do this.

title: You just can't find anything better at this price
text:

Pros:
When I first received them I was surprised by how good and crisp the highs and lows are. The mids are also quite good. These headphones also offer very nice noise cancellation. The highs are probably my favorite part about these headphone as even at high volumes I hear no distortion. The lows are quite balanced and still offer a bit of that puncky thump that so many people search for nowadays. Finally there are the mids. There are so many sounds that these headphones reproduce that other sub $100 headphones just don't offer.

Cons:
There are only a few that I can think of. It doesn't matter what ear piece I use(I use the medium size most of the time as it offers the best seal for my ears) they always feel like they are either too far in my ear or about to fall out. This is quite small and probably doesn't apply to everyone. Also there are some songs where lows get very muddy.

Conclusion:
I have gone through many earbuds in my time and I must say that I have never come across a pair that offer such an amazing price to performance ratio.

title: Best Sleep Headphones I've Tried (Update at end of review)
text:
I fall asleep to audiobooks, and have tried a lot of speakers and headphones with mixed results. My husband bought me these AcousticSheep SleepPhones recently, and what a difference they make! They're very comfortable - okay, the mediums are a little large for me, but I've found a way to position them so they work perfectly. The speakers are thin and pliable, so they're comfortable even if you roll over and lie on them, and the sound is pleasant - not too boomy or too shrill, and you can move the headband so you can listen in both ears or only one, if you prefer.

The one catch is that the wires leading out of the headphones are pretty thin, and judging my previous experience using many headsets and speakers in bed, they're going to break inside at some point. Then I'll either have to order more or perhaps do a little creative wire work and attach new, stronger wires. I'd be perfectly happy to replace these once a year as they've improved my quality of sleep (I'm used to waking when I roll onto a hard plastic speaker or earphone).

BTW, the headband itself is sooo soft and comfy - none of the headbands I've used on my hair over the years are this cozy.

Like it said on the package, these truly are pajamas for your ears ;-)

***Update Feb 9, 2014***

It's been just short of a year since I write the above review. Since then, I ordered a second smaller pair of SleepPhones, the band of which wasn't as soft and furry, but it was good for wearing when doing housework. This one didn't come in the same packaging - the packaging was more minimual. My original pair of SleepPhones' wire on the left ear did indeed break, and I bought a third pair. This was in a much smaller package, but was furry and comfy as the first set. Hopefully it will last a bit longer than my original pair - the wires are a bit more robust.

title: Out of Body Experience
text:
EDM, Electronic Dance Music, has become much more than a genre, it is a culture. These headphones bring it all home.

Open the box and you'll find attractively packaged (hint hint to someone thinking of getting these as a gift) headphones as well as a round case with a zipper matching the color. I chose purple, so the purple and black case is perfect. Inside are an assortment of 3 additional sets of eartips, a small, large (the medium is already attached) and a flanged for deep ear insertion. Fit and proper insertion are key to getting all the sound these headphones offer. The tip goes all the way in the ear canal, forming a seal for optimal sound. When you get the right tip on and insert properly, these are COMFORTABLE and don't slip out. A bonus inside...true to the EDM current, you have all acess as they show the PLUR with a silicone wristband.

The first thing I did was plug it in to my iPhone and listen to Kaskade's Atmosphere. Yes, these are MADE for multi-layered compositions and pulse. Then I made a few calls using them. I prefer my one ear for calls but it's nice to have this option.
Later it was connected to my PC while cruising new tunes. Lest you think they are only for EDM, they really enhance gaming as well.
Then I compared them to my old but loved Lady GaGa Monster Beats, as well as a few lower end headsets. Granted the Beats are getting a little wonky, but I have to say it's better to be in the MEE EDM Universe. Can't help but notice logo similarity, hmmmm.

My mother was great lover of opera and symphony. I grew up listening to her records, and when I was small I'd ask her to put on Ravel's Bolero and I'd lie down, listening to it build.
Need to get out of your skin for a while? Put these on, lie down flat on your back. Hit play, close your eyes, palms up, and just absorb everything.

Now THAT'S kandi for the soul.

title: Less than the sum of its parts
text:
Some products turn out to be better than the sum of their parts. Some go in the opposite direction. This is one of them. While in theory this could have made a great bluetooth earbud headset, it has inexcusable issues for a 2014 product that as of review date costs around seventy bucks. The biggest issues:

1) bluetooth pairing and connectivity. It feels like using one of those old Bluetooth 2.x no-name-brand devices of a few years ago. Pairing doesn't work the first time. Typically you have to turn things on/off until it finally makes a connection. Reconnection with previously paired devices is not always smooth either. Music playback has occasional issues (eg quick resume after a pause sometimes gets you a few seconds of jitteriness before it starts playing normally again). The previous three Jabra bluetooth devices I used were much better than this, even lower priced ones. The same phones/tablets at the same locations work just fine with other bluetooth headsets I use.

2) frustrating ergonomics / user experience. Very few gadgets manage to frustrate me when I use them. This one did. While the earhooks are a good way to keep them in place, putting the set on triggers frustration. Finding the light to see what's going on during pairing means turning them over and over until I notice it. The buttons are too close to the face, whether you wear the cable behind the neck (per the instructions) or in front like a necklace. Not enough tactile difference between the play and two volume buttons.

3) volume increase/decrease steps are too big. Workaround: adjust volume from your phone/tablet

4) annoying beep every single time you press the volume up or down button. Every single press. The beep is useful with the Skip function but not when the volume goes up and down (since you tell the volume is changing, you don't need a beep).

5) the getting started guide is incorrect. Operation is fairly simple actually: To turn on, press and hold the Middle Button until a female computer voice says Hello, then release. If you want to Pair, press and hold until female computer says Pairing, then release. Or if you are starting from Power Off, continue holding the middle button until it enters Pairing Mode. When it enters Pairing Mode, the Light goes in Party Mode (alternating blue and red flashing light - as it is customary with many bluetooth devices). To power off, press and hold the middle button until female computer voice says Goodbye.

But they have some nice features as well:
1) earhooks keep them in place. I think the only time they fell off was when I was bobbing my head sideways trying to see whether they would fall off
2) the earhooks are removable and repositionable. Simply peel them off and move them further down the cable to get a better fit
3) the cable is short enough, you can listen on one ear and put the second earpiece in your shirt pocket or let it rest on your body if sitting
4) the light is semi-discrete, buried underneath the right earpiece, so you don't look like a blinking zombie. On the other hand, it's hard to find when you are trying to see what's going on (power on? pairing mode? etc)

Sound Matters: Music quality is reasonable given the price range and given that this is a bluetooth set designed to stay on your ears. Getting a good fit and seal helps with music quality - trying the three different eartip sizes (included) and adjusting the repositionable earhook may be helpful in this. They leak very little sound to the outside world. Isolation though is about average, they are not as good as other earphones but they do block some of the outside sound.

The volume Up and Down buttons worked with every device I successfully paired them with. The Play/Pause worked with most but not all. Likewise the Next/Previous worked, except sometimes, with some apps on some Android devices, the Previous sometimes takes you to the previous track, sometimes to the beginning of the current track instead. Not sure if it has to do with how long you press and hold the Volume Down button. Typically if you release it after you hear the beep, it goes to the Previous track (except in situations as above). Here's a summary:
* iPod Touch: all okay
* Nexus Android: all okay
* Galaxy Android: all okay
* Prehistoric Android (2.2.x): okay except Previous
* Lumia Windows Phone: all okay

With the Nook with Google Play tablet only the Volume Up/Down and Next work. Surprisingly, not the Play/Pause. With the Samsung Chromebook, only the volume up/down work. With a Tegra 2 Android it fails to pair/connect/work.

UNBOXING: you get the headset, three sizes of eartips, a microUSB to USB charging cable. No AC power adapter. No Jabra app code. No case/pouch.

title: All I can politely write is that what an amazing experience.  freaking AWESOME
text:
All I can politely write is that what an amazing experience. The headphones are small and just sit over the ears (like their noise canceling headphones). The Bluetooth component sits neatly inside the headphones, as we have another Bose Bluetooth headphones and the Bluetooth component sits outside of the headphones. I synced this with iPad, iPhone and iPod Classic (using Kokkia I10). The quality of the sound is fabulous as you would expect from BOSE ( a lot of bass) you will not be disappointed. I played a range of music from rock, pop and classical music...awesomeness is the experience with Bose! The range is not miles...more like 20 feet..and not through too many walls. ...terrific design of compactness and total comfort on my ears. In terms of external noise, it really did cut out the concrete jungle living of traffic hum.

I listened to my music for over an hour now and no pain on my ears...bliss and worth every cent and pennies. I love these new BOSE Bluetooth headphones. Note, they come fully charged. There are little and discreet volume up and down buttons, which are elevated a little so it is easy to find and you will not end up pushing the wrong button. I didn't have to press any additional button to synch..there is a voice telling you that it is seeking to synch..and will let you know when it has connected. There is a button to switch from music to speak on the phone. Crystal clear. It comes with a power charge..a micro USB cable and a RCA cable.(hmm redundant with Bluetooth, but if you have digital piano, you can connect it via the RCA. I am going to get the Bluetooth adaptor to test it with these head phones).

The headphones remember all the names of the gadgets, and will play from which ever one that is 'on', which is a huge plus. There appears to be an intelligence here that we do not see in the Bose over the ear wireless headphones.

In term of play time, after a full charge, which took less than 2 hours: total playtime is more like 8 hours, not 15 hours claimed, but it must be related to the volume too. I had my volume pretty high most of the time. Given, how quickly it charged up, and the number of hours of playtime, I really don't need to charge it up for more than one every three days.
Also comes with a compact and stylish case to store the wires and headphones when not in use.

text: Just got these headphones yesterday and so far I love them! The sound quality is amazing on these headphones, I'm hearing details in the music I've never even noticed before.  It's like the difference between seeing a scene in 2D on a photo or television vs. 3D in real life.  The headphones are also lighter in weight than the Jabra.  The controls are also easy to use while the headphones are still on your head.  Jabra's touch-sensitive controls (work sort of like a laptop trackpad) never worked well, even brand new.  The only downside I've found so far is that my ears hurt if I have the headphones on for more than a couple of hours.  I do have a big head.  The Jabra headphones are also on-ear, but the padding was quite a bit softer and had more give.  The foam on the Bose headphones is definitely stiffer.  I'm going to give it time to see if either the foam becomes less stiff or my ears decide they can handle it, because the sound quality is so good that I am unwilling to return them.

title: Fit and finish are good; nice stowage in provided case
text:
Fit and finish are good; nice stowage in provided case. Replacement ear pads available for about $25.00 USD.

Expensive. As a music headphone, it's OK for routine listening. Sound quality and range is good, and bass response is fine. treble is a little lacking.
Volume/computer controls are intuitive and work correctly. Not comfortable for more than 15 minutes at a stretch, due to inordinate pressure on outer ear. this is worse if one wears glasses. Also, moving about, even within 15 feet of source, creates drop-outs that can be irritating if one enjoys uninterrupted music/podcast content.

As a Bluetooth phone, reception is very good again as long as one remains motionless. Dropouts still occur, and this is not good for business or vital communication. Worse, though, is the very poor microphone that only provides good voice pickup when used with a booming voice. Privacy? Normal speaking voice? Forget that.

Recharge time is OK, a few hours, and run time is good, at about 10. Overall, an expensive product that is not quite ready for consumer use.

title: Well-built and great sounding
text:
These Bose Soundlink Headphones offer a refined wearing experience and well-defined audio reproduction. This set can truly be used as primary headphones in a variety of settings.

Out of the box (and quite an elegant box, I might add), the headphones' 15-hour lithium battery was charged at about 60% of its capacity. This was enough for me to pair and try them immediately with my iPhone 4s. An on-ear headphone attempts to seal the ear openings, rather than creating an acoustical "shell" around the ear. The cushioning was quite soft--not textured like "pleather" but an acoustically open material. "LEFT" and "RIGHT" are designed graphically into the ear-cups themselves, much nicer than the tiny indications typically used.

Pairing was simple: because this was the first device being memorized, the Bose headphones powered on in pairing mode. No pairing codes were required--the headphones exchange their identity over Bluetooth, and a simple tap on their name in the iPhone's Bluetooth preferences panel finished the task. These headphones keep up to eight devices in memory, and the two most recently used devices can be active simultaneously. This helps, for example, when you are listening to audio on a tablet and wish to take a call on your phone.

Since the Bose SoundLink phones have a pair of noise-cancelling microphones built in, you could take that call without removing the headphones. In my test, the microphones worked pretty well, though of course they suffer from being positioned at the ears rather than anywhere near the mouth. Siri voice-control worked well, as long as I spoke loudly and distinctly.

I compared these phones to my working-studio set, the [[ASIN:B00001WRSJ Sony MDRV6 Studio Monitor Headphones with CCAW Voice Coil]]. I use the Sony for everything from recording and cutting interview audio to music mixing, and I like them because they do not add a lot of color to the sound. It would be fair to wonder whether this is an appropriate comparison, wired vs. wireless. Since it's possible to use the Bose phones in a wired mode with an included patch cord, I gave it a whirl.

Compared to the Sony headphones, which are an over-the-ear design, the Bose SoundLink seems a little beefier and direct. Both headphones have great definition and "presence," and I would expect that the Bose phones are tuned for an "end-user" listening to music rather than an audio professional who needs a flat representation of a mix.

Both sets are very comfortable, each in their own way. The on-the-ear design of the Bose SoundLink gives these phones a tougher task to achieve comfort, and Bose seems to have achieved this by wrapping the headband in something like a pillow. I do find the Sony phones more comfortable for long-term wearing, but then again I modified them by replacing the pleather cushions with a velvety cushion, [[ASIN:B0016MF7W2 Beyerdynamic EDT250V Headphone Ear Pads Black]].

The remarkable thing to me about the Bose SoundLink is that there seems to be NO difference between wired and wireless performance. That alone is a huge boost in that there is no tradeoff of performance for the convenience of wire free use.

The controls are intuitive. Placing one's hand over the right ear cup results in the thumb being over the volume and "select" buttons. The select button can be tapped to control music: 1 tap = pause. 2 taps = next track. 3 taps = previous track. Press and hold = ignore incoming call. (with no call coming in, the iOS profiles allow that same button action to call up Siri)

The power/Bluetooth switch is also easy to understand and use. If some devices are already paired, and you want to add another, sliding the button up and holding will put the phones into pairing mode. The button is spring-loaded, so releasing it pushes it back to the "On" position. Pushing up momentarily and releasing "scrolls" among different paired devices. These functions all worked as expected.

Voice prompts are carefully polished and do not "jump" into your ear, nor do they sound coarsely digitized. The voice prompt was able to pronounce the names of each of my devices without sounding like an alien that was about to eat me. :)

In addition to the patch cable (which uses a smaller plug at the headphones end, so it's not an off-the-rack item if you need to replace it), the headphones come with a USB to USB miniB charging cable and a function-shaped case that includes a divider. The ear pads fold to make a smaller package for storage and protection, and the divider serves as a winding holder for the patch cable. Headphones, case, and patch cord all have elements of a slightly-neon blue in their design that contrasts very well with the ubiquitous black base color.

Overall, the Bose SoundLink Headphones are unmistakably high-quality gear, and if uncompromising portability is important to you, I highly recommend them.

title: Sounds as good as my main system
text:
My main system consists of digital preamp, power amp and a pair of ribbon panel speakers; the combined cost is almost like a small sedan. The sound stage is so real that you can "touch" the performers. For serious headphone usage, I use wired AKG or Audio Technica BT. I have a number of earbuds and they are decent for watching movies or phone conversation.

I have a overseas trip coming up but I don't want to bring the big AKG or AT headphones. I have a pair of decent Kiplisch but the mic failed. I was searching for a replacement and this one came up. I bought a Sennheiser earbud for my wife and she is very happy with it though I never tried it myself. I have heard of Sennheiser as a brand but not much else. This one is reasonable in price and so I bought a pair just to try it out.

I must say that I did not like it initially because it sounded so different from the Kiplisch. I thought it was much darker and kind of confined. I let it run for a few hours but not wearing it. Finally, in the evening when I had a chance to sit down to evaluate it. I first tried the Kiplisch and the familiar sound came out. Then I switched to the Sennheiser. It still sounded very different than the Kiplisch but in a good sense. It sounded somewhat like my main system but through this pair of earbud. The sound is rich, balance and detail; the Kiplisch sounds sharp and thin in comparison. I will "break in" this earbud over the next few days. So far so good.

title: The Bluetooth capability did not work with my Note 3 which should be easily compatible with these headphones
text:
Sent back. The Bluetooth capability did not work with my Note 3 which should be easily compatible with these headphones. Tried the headphones in wired mode and was not impressed with the sound either. I'm no audiophile but my old Motorola SD-9 Bluetooth HD headphones blew these out of the water. In fairness to Bluedio, I suppose I just got a bum pair as there are plenty of glowing reviews on this new model already popping up. These may be decent headphones but I'll just tell you now I was really disappointed with the build quality on the whole. Not one thing in either appearance or functionality of the buttons lead me to believe these will hold up over any period of time. I hope I'm wrong, I really wanted to like the product especially given the sweet price point but I'm not interested in trying a replacement.
One thing that may be helpful to prospective purchasers is that in the photos the headphones appear to have a metallic finish over the plastic like the old R and R+ models. This is not the case, the headphones are 100% plastic and look like 100% cheap plastic. On a positive note though they were very comfortable and fit really well but that was quickly negated when I saw how one of the ear cushions was improperly attached and while it was functional, it just looked bad. As I noted, the sound was ok, as in surely adequate but given some of the reviews I was expecting better. What really soured me on the sound though was the fact that sound leakage was really pronounced. Even at moderately low volume settings someone sitting next to you will absolutely hear your music. Sorry Bluedio I really, really, was hopeful and truly wanted to like your product. I've decided to
spend a little bit more and try these: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00DOP3NPW/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

title: With some burn-in, this got better, but still not good enough for what I love to listen to. (Burn-in instruction included)
text:
This is just a first impression of this headphone as it comes out of the box. I'll have updates in a few days of use and then in a few month just to give others a detailed impression of what it is like to own one of these.

First, I bought these used at VERY GOOD condition with Amazon Warehouse Deal, Inc. So it was $158 to began with. Then I got the discount from Prime Saving too, making it a REALLY REALLY worthy buy.
Many's main complain or con about this headphone is the hefty price tag. So right there I have no complaints.

Second, these are complaints in reviews of this model being too soft, not getting loud enough. So that's the first thing I checked out. And I checked it out with wire and on bluetooth. I have realized the problem.
These headphones only gets loud like normal headphones when it's on bluetooth and you turn the volume up as high as you can on the headphone. ON THE HEADPHONE. Then it's like any other wired headphone, listening to it at about 50% of volume is load enough for a quiet room.
BUT, if you tried it wired or didn't turn up the volume on the headphone, then turning the volume up on your computer and phone to about 80% will give you that same result. SO, some people might complain that these headphones just don't get loud enough.
Trust me. If you are using it wireless and have done what I said above, these gets plenty loud.

Third, after playing a few songs I knew cheap headphone don't do justice to, I can say this pair is sounding pretty good out of the box. The strength is in the mid-range. Instruments like cello sounds amazing on these!
But the bass is really weak, almost not there, and there is sibilance (the uncomfortable "tsh" sound with any mid-high range sounds). I can't really stand listening to female vocals on this right now.
Though I expect the quality will go up after burn-in. Personally, I have always found the Sennheiser headphones needs to be burned in to sound better. It's seems especially true for this pair.
I know some will argue that Burn-In does nothing, but from personal experience, burn-in opens up the sound stage, boost the base, and takes away the tsh sounds. And it's not my ears adjusting to the way the headphone sounds, because when I burn-in, I put it aside and let it go through the sound track on its own. That sound track consisting of Pink and White noise, Frequency Sweeps, and bass heavy tracks like Dubstep and "Silent Shout" by The Knife.

For burn-in here is my steps:
1. For the first 2 hours I let it play at about 50% volume on a mid-range focused song, like Country, or R&B, with male vocalists or female vocalist with a deeper voice. This is a good time to play Pink and White noises.
2. For the next 2 hours I let it play at about the same volume on a classical string sound track to open the higher ranges. Pick good orchestras and good soundtracks because a badly recorded soundtrack doesn't do justice to the high notes.
3. For the next 10 minutes I let the headphone rest.
4. For the next 2 hours i let it play at about 60-65% volume with base heavy music. But an better alternative is taiko drum. I have found them the best way to open up the base response on headphones.
5. Let the Headphone take a break and then start from Step 1 again.

You can stop burn-in at any time to test the quality. Doing one of the above step longer if you feel like a certain range is weaker, and you are satisfied with another.
After a day or two, you are ready to test these babies again! Tell me you don't hear a difference! I'm at the first stage of burn-in. Will report in a few days.
Something to remember, the more you listen on these headphones, the better they'll sound. The burn-in continues withe use. So you don't have to burn them in with above steps. But I just can't stand how poor the bass is.

------------

I tried.
But this pair of headphone's bass response is just not on par with what I'm looking for. I have been spoiled by my ATH-M50. I love listening to Jazz, which requires a pretty open stage and open bass. The bass got better, stronger with burn-in, but not enough.
And compared to my ATH-M50, the stage isn't that open at all. (Both closed headphones).
I'm not a heavy bass lover, but I require a balanced amount of it to enjoy the type of music I listen to.
Having heard them a certain way for sometime, listening to the same song on here is a bit disappointing.

I wouldn't be keeping these after all.

title: Decent headphone for traveling
text:
This is a very decent set of headphones for traveling. I bought these as an "upgrade" to my old pair of Bose because of the noise cancellation feature and the sound quality. While the noise cancellation on these headphones is not 100%, it is more than sufficient for airplane travel and keeps out most of the background vibration, muffles unwanted conversation, crying babies etc.

It has an added feature called SRS that makes the sound a bit crisper. This is especially useful when the noise cancellation feature is engaged, as this can be lost when the background noise is loudest.

It has a rechargeable battery that is more than sufficient to do a long haul overseas flight. It charges on a standard USB phone charger. The earphones also have a built in volume feature and bluetooth connectivity for wireless use if you want to run it off your phone. One of my favorite features is a "mute" button that actually silences the music and engages an external microphone so you can hear announcements or people talking to you without having to remove the headphones.

My only issue - and its a minor one - is that the ear covers are very well padded which means they get very warm from your body heat after extended use - sort of an earmuff effect. Otherwise though it's the best set of headphones i've owned

title: Extremely impressed with noise canceling abilities
text:
I've used the ATH-ANC7B on several flights and have found that they do an excellent job blocking ambient noises -- specifically the drone of the plane's engines and HVAC system -- making it possible to listen to music, podcasts and movies with the volume set to normal levels. Even quiet passages in movies and music come through well -- never any need to jack up the volume.

On my most recent flight, the HVAC system was turned up so insanely high that the ambient sound level on the plane -- according to an app on my iPhone -- was 94dB! That's the same level of noise you hear standing 30 feet from a motorcycle. But the ATH-ANC7B reduced it to a mild hum and I was able to watch a movie with no problem. Whenever I took the headphones off it was jarring just how loud the plane really was.

Sound Quality: When listening on a plane the quality is perfectly good. But I wouldn't use them as everyday headphones. In a quiet environment the headphones' shortcomings come out. Compared to sub-$100 Sennheiser headphones I own, the sound is distant, lacks presence, and is not is clear. In a noisy environment, such as a plane, the ambient sounds that still comes through masks these shortcomings. So if you're going to primarily use these headphones in places like an airplane, you won't notice these issues.

Comfort: The headphones clamp on to your ears tight -- the close fit is a component of how they block ambient sounds. Yet, I haven't experienced any discomfort. I've worn them for 2.5 hours straight -- an entire movie -- and I never felt the need to remove them to give my ears a rest.

Comparison to the Bose QuietComfort 15: The Bose QC 15 is the gold standard in noise canceling headphones. Having used them on a plane, I feel that they did a slightly better noise cancellation job, but not such a better job to justify being nearly three times as expensive. And what really concerns me about the Bose is not the price, but the replacement cost. That is, spending $300 dollars on an audio component isn't an issue, it's $300 on something that is prone to breaking. Headphones are relatively fragile. People bang in to them, wires get caught and ripped, etc. Very quickly a $300 investment can turn into $600.

Bottom line: Audio-Technica's ATH-ANC7B help making flying a lot more pleasurable. Highly recommended.

title: Disappointed
text:
To date, I've bought EIGHT sets of Bose speakers for my computers at home and at work. I've never owned a "premium" headphone set so after reading over reviews decided on a used pair of Bose (AE2). I tested them on the same track on my Iphone, same song, against a cheap-o $5 (no joking) Dollar General earbuds with mic. I thought I'd made a mistake connecting the Bose factory cord to the head unit because the sound quality was so much WORSE on the Bose over-ear speakers than on the Dollar General super-cheap in-ear speakers. On the Dollar General speakers, I hear a rich, deep bass. And the vocals are crystal clear. I feel like I'm at a live concert--without all the screaming of fans around me. But on the Bose, I feel like I'm outside on the sidewalk hearing the music that escapes the concert hall into the streets. I checked three times to be sure I was actually using a set of Bose--thinking I'd been sent a bogus pair. Yup, these are Bose. With the factory cord!

I also ordered an after-market mic-cord to use with these headphones, turning them into the Bose AE2i. The sound quality was just about the worst I've ever, ever experienced with headphones. Tinny and cheap--what you'd expect from a $2 pair of Walmart generic headphones. Stunned. The aftermarket mic-headphone cable and the used Bose AE2 headset are both going back.

Now I don't know what to do. Do I spend $500 on a set of "high quality" headphones when my earbuds for one-percent of that work great? I thought over-the-ear headphones would be much more comfortable (they are) and, with bigger drivers, sound much better (not by a long shot--at least not these Bose). But the additional comfort is not worth hundreds of dollars, especially for lower sound quality. I guess I'll go into a factory to test headphones in person. Doesn't seem like I can buy something that relies so much on personal taste online even with lots of reviews.

My advice: don't assume a big-name over- or on-the-ear headphone set will be better than your cheap in-ear headphones that form a seal inside your ear canal and so deliver sound directly to your ears directly.

I'm super-disappointed in Bose. :(

title: Tough, comfortable, great sound.
text:
I'm not an audiophile, but I am a singer (and former music major), and I received these headphones as a Christmas present from my not-so-wealthy family who gave them to me as my main gift. Although the sound seemed to be a step back from my earphones and there is a bit of leaking - and it took me ages to actually use them! - what I found was absolutely amazing.

Not only does the bass sound great without compromising the quality of the mid and low sounds (I'm looking at you, Skullcandy), but the headphones are extremely portable, bendable, manipulatable, comfortable, and just plain durable. The wire is extremely resistant to bending/breaking and the whole thing has actually survived being stepped on once. I shove them in my purse and have ported them around in pockets and on bus rides. They're monsters.

Note: if you notice the sound getting dull or flickering, check where the wire is plugged into your audio device AND the headphones themselves. I missed that jack until I pulled it out and panicked that I'd broken my headphones, but upon adjusting it the sound improved a lot. The design is excellent in that regard, too, because the cord can take a lot of manhandling.

I don't know if they're necessarily the best headphones in the world (again, not an audiophile or even super knowledgable), but they are the best I've ever had.

title: Amazed from the first few seconds of listening
text:

You know you've found a nice set of phones when you listen to a song you are really familiar with and almost immediately you find yourself saying, "Wow. I never heard that before."

I'm mainly using them to listen to my keyboard synth which plays a wide variety of sounds including grand pianos, drums, strings, vocals, screaming guitars, etc. More than once when playing late at night, I've quickly removed the headphones to make sure I hadn't forgotten to turn the speakers off. Somehow, you can actually feel the bass in your chest with these phones. Seems impossible, I know, but it caught me off guard twice before I accepted that it was the headphones.

Lastly, the comfort level of these phones is awesome. They are very light, almost impossibly so when you factor in the sound they produce. I can easily wear them for hours comfortably. And while these are not noise-cancelling headphones, the cushion and around the ear fit are so good that you do decrease surrounding sound significantly.

Highly recommended.

title: It Is a Clamp Your Head and Ears Device
text:
I currently have a Sony DR-BT22, a MDR-A30 and a MDR-W24. I also had a countless number of Sony headphones and earphones from the good old days. The Sony's from the good old days sounded really great.

I try to find one that is as good as any of the Sony. This Koss KPH14W is not it.

The spec printed on the box is as follows.
3.5 mm plug
4 feet long cord
100 - 15,000 Hz
18 Ohms
104 dB SPL

This Koss sounds average at best. I think the best I can describe the differences is that the Sony's sound like an expensive 2.1 speaker system with clean sound and house-shaking bass. The Koss is just a very average 2.0 speaker system. It is not FM/AM radio bad. It is just average. Your car radio sounds better.

The fit of the Koss is very bad. It is for kid with small head. The Koss is at least an inch shorter than the Sony. The plastic material is hard plastic. It clamps to my head and inside my ears so tight. It hurts. Compared the plastic from the Sony, the Sony uses soft flexible rubbery plastic. The Sony is soft like a pillow but very supportive at the same time.

I have to follow the advice from the other reviewers. I use my hair dryer to soften the plastic. So, I can bent it wider. Even it is wider, it is still too short and not comfortable.

On the positive side, the Koss has the longest cord. It is 4 feet long. The plug is in a 140 degree angle.

I have some pictures. The white one is the Koss. The picture with the Koss inside the packaging is how tight it is. It is a clamp. You can see how wide I have to bent it to fit better.

I cannot recommend this Koss. It is too small for an adult and the sound is just average.

title: Great Noise Cancelling Headphones
text:
My work bought each person in my branch a pair of QC25’s from Amazon. I also own a set of QC2’s.

I have to say, whether I’m wearing my QC25’s or QC2’s, I love my Bose QC headsets and will not travel without them. I also use them for work, not just at work.

Since I have both a pair of the old and new, I thought I’d do my own comparison:

1. Equally comfortable

2. In a quiet environment, where noise cancelling isn’t really a factor, I think the sound quality (even of the older QC2’s) is pretty comparable. If I were thinking about upgrading just for sound quality, I don’t think I would.

3. Noise cancelling has definitely improved in the QC25’s over the older QC2’s. In a noisey environment where noise cancelling matters, the difference is noticeable. The QC2’s are good, the QC25’s are clearly better.

4. The QC25’s will work w/o a battery. If the battery dies in the QC25, you will have music, just not NC. In the older QC2’s, the headphones would not work at all w/a dead or no battery.

5. QC25’s have a mic for taking or making phone calls. The QC2’s did not.

6. The case is smaller, but just as protective for the QC25’s. The QC2’s do not fold up as small.

7. They both look good.

8. The prices really haven’t changed over the years.

The bottom line, I love my Bose headsets, both of them. I would absolutely recommend buying a set, particularly if you have a need for a set of quality headphones at work or for travel.

For me, after reviewing the older and newer QC headsets, I don’t think I’d upgrade until the older QC2’s stopped working. I think that Bose headsets are built so well, that time doesn’t diminish the quality and utility of Bose’s older products.

title: Isolate your ears and light up your mind
text:
Upgraded to the QC25 from the very popular ~$35 Sony noise cancelling headset that you can find on Amazon. The difference is spectacular, which is very welcome considering the "slight" difference in price. An amazing piece of technology that is of exceptional sturdiness and quality. I got the Samsung version and the in-line cable controls work perfectly for my Galaxy S6 Edge.

On to the actual quality of the main feature. The leather ear covers are soft, sweat/oil repellent, and don't leave any marks on my skin afterwards. The inside of the ear cups are slightly curved, I'm assuming so that the sound is project more directly into your ear. I have quite large, protruding ears and these fit perfectly. The noise cancelling feature is outstanding - I am sitting next to an aquarium with multiple fans, pumps and filters on and if I was blindfolded I wouldn't be able to tell you if I was in my room or in the middle of a park. Sound quality is the best of any headphone I've ever used, leagues above any stock earbuds. You will hear the individual piano keys being struck in a classical piece, and the subtle breathing inflections of a singer.

title: BoseSoundTrue around-ear headphones II
text:
When I shop for headphones, I shop primarily for comfort. I’m not a sound snob -- I just need headphones that are super comfortable.

I’ve had a few pairs of over-ear/around-ear headphones. If I wear them too long, they give me a headache, either because they are too heavy after a while or squeeze too much or both. My last was a pair of Skullcandy’s, Hesh style, and I couldn’t wear them for more than 2-3 hours. These Bose SoundTrue’s feel a little lighter, and the ear cups are oval, not round, which makes them fit me better. They also don’t feel as tight on my head as the Skullcandy’s, but I don’t feel like they’re going to fall off.

Soundwise, I think they’re fine. But as I said, I’m not a sound snob, so as long as music sounds good and not like it’s played through a tin can, I’m happy.

Convenience wise, the ear cups swivel so the headphones fit in the included flat case. They don’t fold up a lot, but the case will be handy for when I want to take the headphones out with me. The cord is detachable, and has a remote for music/phone call control. I received the Apple version to review, so only the play/pause worked on my phone, but the other functions worked on my Macbook Air.

title: Fantastic lightweight headphones that can also be used for calls
text:
The Bose SoundTrue is a lightweight headphone that has crisp clear sound and also works as a phone headset thanks to an inline mic with a 3 button remote. The bass is rich, but probably not enough if you like it thumping a lot. There isn’t any distortion and it does a good job of isolating ambient noise. I’m impressed by the sound quality for the price.

The inline buttons can be used for answering calls or for skipping through audio files. It even works to skip tracks on Spotify. It folds flat for storage and comes in a nice compact zip case, as it should for this price. I like that the cable detaches for storage, and is hence replaceable – although the replacement is pretty pricey. But in my experience, the cord is usually the weakest link and it will be cheaper to replace that than the entire headset.

title: Good clear audio quality and a nice fit without a lot of weight
text:
The sound quality of the around-ear headphones is clear and crisp. I used the headphones with two different android phones (don't forget to pair the devices with the headphone), an iphone, android tablet, laptop (windows 7 OS), and an mp3 player. All had consistently good audio quality except that our bluetooth headsets when used by the call-ER added reverberation, echoes, and backgound static -- without the call-ER using the headset the sound was clear again. (SO, I'm blaming the headset not the headphones.)

Using the headphones without being plugged into a device to give you audio. severely dampens the ambient noise -- making any internal sounds very noticeable (such as breathing and heartbeat and other body noises). Thus, using the headphones with an MP3 player while walking or jogging could keep you from hearing approaching cars -- if this is what you plan to use the headphones for be very vigilant..

The fit is nice and the headphones are labeled L for the left ear and R for the right ear. The only real problem with the headphone is one that as far as I can tell happens with most around-ear headphones is they keep your ears very warm causing condensation and dampness around the ears. I'm thinking they may be better than my in-ear headset during the winter for my daily walks listening to my MP3 player, especially on cold days -- but I'll really have to pay attention to my surroundings because these headphones really deaden external sound (which is a nice feature if you're *not* out walking near traffic).

There's a volume control (which didn't seem to do anything when used so we used the device volume control and that worked fine. I'm not sure why I had this problem so, I think it was operator error -- I may have been moving the sound down rather than up because the control is on the plugin cord and I couldn't really see it clearly and if you don't have the cord in the right orientation to do what you want it to, you'll be doing the opposite of what you want when you press the switch. It was easier for me to just use the device volume control on the phone, notepad, MP3 player or whatever. The answer button on the cord did seem to work okay and it paired with the phones.

title: Oh, if they only had noise cancellation....
text:
This is an excellent product that could have been improved by optional noise cancellation.

I cannot complain about the latter, because it is not a feature of the unit and it is not specified as one. I just think it would be great on the plane or bus when I travel.

Other than that, the microphone and headset are great. The noise level is low on the microphone, so I can talk over it easily. The only issue I have is noise in the background when in a noisy environment. And that is not the fault of the headset, but the lack of a feature.

The headset independent of that limitation is amazing. The sound is the best I have ever heard on earbuds. The bass is astounding. The clarity is as well. The microphone works wonderfully in almost all situations except truly excessive background noise.

However, the most astounding aspect is the bluetooth is flawless. I have not found a situation in which I could not receive a clear signal and clear sound. It may be impacted by background noise, but it is never the wireless connection.

These sound better than some over the ear headsets I have. Quality, feel, fit, etc. are all fantastic.

Noise reduction is required for environments that are not background friendly. If you are more interested in listening to music and conducting wireless chat in a controlled environment or at least one not exposed to extreme background noise, these are the ticket.

title: An excellent headset-microphone for Speech Recognition
text: I purchased this microphone/headphone because I needed something that would work with Window's voice recognition software.  I had injured my hand and was unable to type for over a month, so I was going to have to dictate to my computer for a while.  It was not something I was looking forward to, since in the past I have found the software to be somewhat “glichy”, and more trouble than it was worth.  However this time I had no choice.  I first tried to use a standalone microphone, but I discovered that it was not very good at picking up my voice, and created lots of neck and back problems since I had to keep bending down to get my mouth as close to the microphone as possible.  Therefore I thought perhaps a headphone microphone would work better, and also give me more freedom of movement.  I researched many different headphone-microphones, many of which had bad reviews for being flimsy in construction as well as bad electronics.  However I tried this unit, and I must say I was quite pleased.  Yes it is not extremely solid in construction, yet is quite light on the head which is important if you’re gonna keep it on most of the day.  The headphones are indeed stereo, and I have learned to enjoy the intimacy of music and other computer audio.  Most important however is that the microphone is quite sensitive, and I realized that the speech recognition software is not as bad as I thought, it was just the quality of the microphone I was using before was not picking up my voice correctly.  However this microphone, which is easily adjustable, does a great job of picking up the voice, and I find a 90% reduction in mistaken text from my dictation.  In fact, this review is being "dictated" using this unit! For the price this is really a great unit.  Of course if one is looking for sound with a booming bass, then I suggest buying specific headphones for that purpose.  This is fine for me however and the reason for the purchase really has to do with the voice recognition, which it does perfectly.  Its software downloads to your computer easily with the USB port (and a very generous cable length),and the interface between the headphones, the computer, and either Window's built-in speech recognition software, or any other software you may purchase is carefree.  It is truly “plugged and go”! No need to look any further for these needs than this Koss Headset-Microphone..

title: Works well, even the HRM is pretty accurate (when measured against my other HRM's at same time)
text:
So I actually have 4 heart rate monitors, I have the Polar H7 HRM, the Samsung Icon X (w/HRM), Atlas fitness watch (w/HRM) and a fitbit Charge 2 (w/HRM). I know, it's over kill, but what better way to determine if your devices are accurate or not then to compare them with other HRM's at the same time? Well I took all 4 to the gym today and I hit the cardio machine and exercised for 60 minutes and set each device to log my HRM in their respective apps. Throughout my workout, the Polar, Samsung and the Atlas fitness watches were all within +- 2 heart beats from each other (150-165 beats) while the fitbit hung in there for about the first 15 minutes of the workout then after that the display was showing my heart rate at least 30 beats behind the others then after about 30 minutes my heart rate on the fitbit was a good 80 heart beats behind then shortly after that it stopped measuring my heart rate completely, Off and on and it would show a heart rate through out the remaining workout, but it was showing it only in the 50-70 range while the other 3 devices were showing my heart rate in the 155-160 range.

Chest HRM's are supposed to be one of the more accurate ways to measure your heart rate when exercising and seeing that 3 of the 4 HRM's I had were all within a couple heart beats from each other makes me believe the Polar (and the Samsung and Atlas) are fairly accurate in their readings. The fitbit, well, if it wasn't for the auto sleep profiling, that one would be going back to the store since it doesn't seem to be very accurate for it's intended purpose, being a fitness watch.

All in all, i'm very pleased with the Polar H7 HRM and I'll continue to use that for my cardio exercises and I'll rely on the atlas and Samsung when i'm doing weight exercises since wearing a strap is a bit annoying to me when i'm lifting weights. The fitbit... well... if I don't return it, it'll just be relegated to being a sleep monitor and that's it as I don't trust it for measuring anything else.

As for the Icon X, the sounds are pretty good. I sync'd my music to the ear phones instead of using Bluetooth so that the battery life would be longer. I like that the HRM seems pretty accurate, it actually surprised me that it was within 1-2 heart beats of the chest strap for my entire workout. One thing that annoyed me though was that everytime I took my towel to wipe some sweat off my face, everytime the town hit the Icon X ear bud, it would register as a touch and it would pause my music... ugh.. but after a few times of doing that, I became aware of it and made sure not to go near it :) The fit was pretty good for my ears too, not once did I ever feel like it would slip out and fall and it stayed nice and snug in my ears. Really, other than the price, I have no complaints about these ear buds.

I did buy my icon x from a B&M store, but I felt like some people might benefit from reading about my experiences with it, especially how accurate the HRM function appears to be. The only thing I didn't like was that if I used the s health app to monitor my heart rate using the icon x, I could no longer set up the exercise mode in the icon x. It seems you can either use the icon x exercise mode or you can do real time sync with the s health app but not both at the same time. not really a big deal but I was curious to see what the icon x coaching was like but I didn't want to stop my s health monitoring since I was using that to compare the HRM function of this with the other 3 HRM's I was wearing at the same time. Maybe next time I'll give it a try though :)

I know, it's over kill, but what better way to determine if your devices are accurate or not then to compare them with other HRM's at the same time? Well I took all 4 to the gym today and I hit the cardio machine and exercised for 60 minutes and set each device to log my HRM in their respective apps. Throughout my workout, the Polar, Samsung and the Atlas fitness watches were all within +- 2 heart beats from each other (150-165 beats) while the fitbit hung in there for about the first 15 minutes of the workout then after that the display was showing my heart rate at least 30 beats behind the others then after about 30 minutes my heart rate on the fitbit was a good 80 heart beats behind then shortly after that it stopped measuring my heart rate completely, Off and on and it would show a heart rate through out the remaining workout, but it was showing it only in the 50-70 range while the other 3 devices were showing my heart rate in the 155-160 range.

Chest HRM's are supposed to be one of the more accurate ways to measure your heart rate when exercising and seeing that 3 of the 4 HRM's I had were all within a couple heart beats from each other makes me believe the Polar (and the Samsung and Atlas) are fairly accurate in their readings. The fitbit, well, if it wasn't for the auto sleep profiling, that one would be going back to the store since it doesn't seem to be very accurate for it's intended purpose, being a fitness watch.

All in all, i'm very pleased with the Polar H7 HRM and I'll continue to use that for my cardio exercises and I'll rely on the atlas and Samsung when i'm doing weight exercises since wearing a strap is a bit annoying to me when i'm lifting weights. The fitbit... well... if I don't return it, it'll just be relegated to being a sleep monitor and that's it as I don't trust it for measuring anything else.

As for the Icon X, the sounds are pretty good. I sync'd my music to the ear phones instead of using Bluetooth so that the battery life would be longer. I like that the HRM seems pretty accurate, it actually surprised me that it was within 1-2 heart beats of the chest strap for my entire workout. One thing that annoyed me though was that everytime I took my towel to wipe some sweat off my face, everytime the town hit the Icon X ear bud, it would register as a touch and it would pause my music... ugh.. but after a few times of doing that, I became aware of it and made sure not to go near it :) The fit was pretty good for my ears too, not once did I ever feel like it would slip out and fall and it stayed nice and snug in my ears. Really, other than the price, I have no complaints about these ear buds.

I did buy my icon x from a B&M store, but I felt like some people might benefit from reading about my experiences with it, especially how accurate the HRM function appears to be. The only thing I didn't like was that if I used the s health app to monitor my heart rate using the icon x, I could no longer set up the exercise mode in the icon x. It seems you can either use the icon x exercise mode or you can do real time sync with the s health app but not both at the same time. not really a big deal but I was curious to see what the icon x coaching was like but I didn't want to stop my s health monitoring since I was using that to compare the HRM function of this with the other 3 HRM's I was wearing at the same time. Maybe next time I'll give it a try though :)
