title: Gear IconX are great cord-free earbuds!
text:
I have been using/testing the Samsung Gear IconX wireless earbuds for about a month now. I love these things and they have made my walking activity much more enjoyable! While the earbuds are primarily pushed as fitness headphones, they work well as a mobile music player. The charging case can hold up to 1,000 songs. I have about 120 songs that I've downloaded to the device which a lot more space available.

I was able to charge and use the earbuds out of the box. They come with additional tips to adjust for a more comfortable and snug fit. Whether it's walking or doing crunches and lunges, the earbuds stayed put.

The touch controls took a little getting used to, but once I got the hang of the pressure I applied to the touch pad it was a breeze. I like being able to switch through songs without feeling as though my workout activity is being majorly interrupted.

There is great sound quality coming through. I am not a fan of the ambient sound feature. When on, there seems to be too much extra noise and I can hear every step I take or move I make. It was somewhat annoying so I do not use that feature, but can still hear my surroundings without it being turned on.

I use the earbuds in conjunction with the Gear Fit2 so I have not primarily used them for the fitness tracking aspect. However, the one time I did use it for this purpose, the tracking seemed to be accurate so I have no complaints. However, using the Gear IconX with the Gear Fit2 is a great pairing.

I've also used the earbuds as my wireless headset for my office phone that utilizes VoIP software through the computer. A quick connection to the Bluetooth and I can enjoy music without disturbing others in the office and still get phone calls that come through. Another great feature that I've enjoyed!

I would recommend these to anyone looking for a decent quality, cord-free earbud to use with any type of exercise or other activity when one wants to listen to music and/or track their physical activity.

They also cannot pair without the proprietary Gear app, only available on phones at the time. I couldn't use them when I use my tablet at the gym.

I lost my earbuds a month after purchase. The charging case is convenient to store in a pocket, but impossible to find if it falls out or you forget where you placed them. Samsung needs to add a Bluetooth tracking feature to the case so they are easier to find if lost. Definitely room for improvement!

title: The best "kernel buds" I've tested
text:
These are far better than I expected them to be. To begin with, I have no interest in the health features. My interest was in active noise cancelling and sound quality in a great form factor and these deliver.

As another reviewer mentioned, these seal the ear canal so you will hear a thumping as you walk, run, or do any activity that is jarring. This is one of the reasons Comply foam tips are so great. They seal the ear canal but because they are foam, air can escape so you don’t get the thumping. (it is equivalent to the pressure thumping you get in the car when you roll down just one window a crack)

Pros:
• Very comfortable, even after 2 hours (which is when the battery died)
• Great sound. Mostly mid-range but good bass and treble. They sounded better than the “gear circle” headphones I had and they are on par with many other higher end headsets. They sound as good as my 1st generation LG Tone Infinums.
• The capsule (charging case) is small and comfortable enough to carry in your pocket, purse, or bag.
• Charge quickly in the case.
• Comply foam tips fit but… (see cons)
• Active noise cancellation and you can manage that from the phone app
• Great phone app

Cons:
• Battery lasts only a couple of hours (about 2 on average in my experience)
• As I said, the Comply ear tips fit but then you can’t close them in the charging case with them on so you are left with three options:
o Forget the Complys and get the “thumps” from the standard tips if you are active
o Take them on and off between charging (ridiculous, too much work)
o Cut about 2-3 millimeters off the Comply foam tips so they will fit in the charging case (this is what I did and I am happy with this choice)
• When I use only on ear piece (audiobooks that are mono or if I’m using the phone). The signal cuts out a lot just by turning my head too far to the left or right if my phone is in my pocket.
o Interestingly, this does not happen at all if both headsets are in.

Final notes:
• Ambient sound is a great option for running or walking as you want to hear cars, etc. but you can turn it off so the active noise cancellation can cut out much of the noise of your lawn mower or blower.
• I cannot recommend these for air travelers as the battery won’t last more than 2 hours or so and it would be so easy to drop one and lose it.
Overall, happy with them

title: Completely useless. Any cheap $10 set on Amazon is better than these.
text:
These would be fine, but the battery life makes them useless. When linked to your phone, you get about two hours of life out of them. You can double that by using only one at a time, but it isn't as simple as putting the used one back in the charger, and putting the other one in your ear. In order to switch which headphone you are using, you need to open up the Samsung Gear app, and switch from there. BOTH headphones need to be in your ear and have battery life in order to do this. The whole process takes about one minute to do the swap. That doesn't seem too bad, but when you are exercising and have to stop what you are doing for over a minute, it gets frustrating. If the headphone you are using dies before the swap, you CAN NOT use the other headphone, even if it is fully charged.

The battery case that holds the headphones and charges them doesn't have great capacity either. It can charge both of the headphones once, but it quickly loses charge over time. If you fully charge both the headphones and case, unplug them, and try to use them 24 hours later, all three batteries will be fully drained. So, the only option is to leave it plugged in at all times when not in use, but the documentation specifically warns you not to do this, because it will wear on the battery over time.

Also, if the case's battery dies, but your headphones both have a charge, the headphones sometimes won't turn off if you store them in the case, because they think they are still in your ear, meaning they will continue to drain their batteries.

I've used multiple different $10 cheap Chinese wireless headphones from Amazon, and ALL of them were better than this.

title: A decade with the ER4S
text:
My pair of ER4S is about to turn 10 years old. I thought enough time had passed to finally write an Amazon review. Heh heh. I was the second person on Headwize.com (before there was a Head-Fi) to get them and post comments. I've used a seemingly endless number of headphones over the years: Sennheiser HD580, Denon 950, Sony 7509, Sony 7506, Sony MDR600, Koss ESP950 electrostatics, about half a dozen Koss dynamic headphones, one pair of Stax, Ixos' top of the line 1001, Pioneer's top of the line DJing headphones, two models of AKG studio headphones, JVC's former top of the line (only available direct), HN-7506, both versions of the Extreme Isolation UR-29, and a seemingly unending number of cheapos bundled with music players.

Whew! So what do I think about the Etymotic Research ER4S? I think it is frankly without peer amongst those cans I've heard. It is flat, transparent, resolved, extended, dynamic, fast, tight, totally grain-free, and impossible to distort. It is not capable of the inner-light of, say, Pierre Gabriel of Quebec's loudspeaker systems, or the sheer delicacy, finesse, and seeming perfection of Burmeister of Germany's loudspeakers. But those are, after all, loudspeakers. I've never heard any headphones achieve what those two audiophile names have. And yes, I have listened to them thoroughly and been marveled. If you question my ears, I was the only person in a room run by Thiele at CES (filled with audiophiles and magazine writers) to point out repeatedly and correctly when the active cabling technology was changed without us seeing.

People all have different tastes. We all have different hearing responses, even if slight. Our ear canals vary. And on and on. Your results may vary. But when I can take some of the most lauded DJ mixers and compare them adequately using such a relatively inexpensive piece of gear when heretofore it was only possible to do such comparisons on large nightclub sound systems, I feel pretty confident the little Etys are doing enough right to recommend them. Over time, I have found the black foam earpieces to give the best sound and comfort, but the white rubber flanged tips certainly isolate better, which if there's background noise is more beneficial to the sound than anything else. Years ago, I preferred the sound of the flange tips. Maybe I have hearing loss? Maybe I just didn't test the foam ones enough? Don't know, but they come with both, so you have no excuse not to try both. You can also get larger yellow foam ones and smaller blue flanged rubber tips. I tried the blues recently and they were too small to seal properly.

A word of advice on the flanged tips, use a dab of water on them, pull your ear up slightly, and put it in so the edge of the flanges are the same depth on both ears. After a few minutes, assuming you don't have ear problems, the pressure of the air between the earphone and the eardrum will equalize since the tympanic membrane is slowly permeable to air. If there's not much bass, you don't have it in deep enough, you need a better headphone jack, or the source device sucks. Most MP3 players have poor headphone jacks, so don't blame the Ety for having an impedance of 100ohms and wanting a touch more of current capability. In spite of that, they still sound impressive connected even to cheap gear. I have a $40 portable CD player with a monster headphone jack that, combined with the Ety, you'd have to pay a significant sum to keep me from using on airline flights. It makes flying not only tolerable, but something to look forward to.

title: Great headphones. Expensive.
text:
These headphones are fantastic. I guess I took a star off because for the money, these should be perfect, and there are just a few small issues.

Pros:

-Great fit, great options for ear tips.

Cons:
-Stick straight out of the ear canals - can't sleep in them or wear under a beanie, and any pull on the cables really torques in your ears!
-Picks up wind - the braided cable and the part of the bud sticking from the ear both pick up wind noise. Not for riding on your bike!
-Expensive

Overall, though, they are fantastic. The sound is almost unparalleled. If the shape of the ear bud is not to you liking, I would recommend the Shure E315. Similar in terms of comfort, quality of sound, and variety of ear tips, but the cables go up and over your ear, reducing some of the issues with wind and fit. But overall, I would call it a draw between the two.

running -- lots of *thump* *thump* *thump* from the cord bouncing on your chest.
sound -- superb.
durability -- not so much.

title: I Took the Pepsi Challenge
text:
Pulp Fiction Metaphorical Comparison...

LANCE (to Vincent):

"...Now this is Panda [ER-6], from Mexico. Very good stuff. This is Bava [ER-6i], different, but equally good. And this is Choco [ER-4P] from the Hartz Mountains of Germany....but this one...(pointing to the Choco)...this one's a little more expensive...But when you shoot it, you'll know where that extra money went..."

IMHO, the same can be said about the ER4P's: You'll know where the extra money went. Spending the extra $$$ is well worth it. Yes, I've purchased all three (for my iPod) and settled on the BBME (biggest-best-most EXPENSIVE). My hunt for a fantastic IE set has finally come to an end. Keep in mind, before experimenting with the Etymotic series, I've previously owned Sony's (MDR-EX71SL & MDR-EX81SL) and onto Sennheiser (CX300's). If you're on a budget and like lots of bass, the CX300 top both Sony models.

As far as the Etymotic are concerned, my first purchase was the ER-6. While I'm sure with a proper fit and amplification, they are great. However, with my iPod, and a poor fit with the flanges, and mediocre fit with the foam, I gave up. Because of a poor fit, they sounded like faint tin cans. PROPER fit is a MUST for any IE headphone to function correctly.

Manufactured specifically for small media players, I tried the ER6i. The triple flange when wet, fit snugly and sealed well. It is important to follow the directions to acheive a proper fit. There was a huge difference in sound over the previous. After listening to them for two days, I tried my old CX300's on and found out how artifical the bass was, and how they muddied the sound. The same cannot be said for the ER6i's. While I found the bass to be lighter, I didn't mind, and managed my EQ to adjust (R & B worked best). I've read complaints about the bass, especially when listening to rap. I don't agree. I found it very satisfactory. The ER6i's are worth the money if you cannot afford the Choco...

At twice the price of the ER6i's the ER-4P's better offer something special-and they do! Extra accessories aside, the sound was unmatched by the above. I tested both without any EQ at the same volume level. While the ER6i's were a little more punchy in the bass and had a warmer overall tone, the ER4P's walked all over them as far as a realistic presentation of the music. What did I find? Clarity, near flawless sound & tonality, and just enough bass to keep me happy. An EQ adjustment back to R & B brought up the bass a little, and took a little of the edge off the high end.

To conclude, if you're willing to shell out the big bucks, then go for the ER-4's. However, the ER-6i's are well worth the price ($10-$20 more than the CX300's), especially if you're on a budget. Either way, you can't go wrong, but for me, I'll stick with the Choco.

title: 10 year Etymotic user
text:
I got my first ER4S set 10 years ago and a second set a couple of years later to ensure that I would not be without some Etymotics. Both sets are fine after all this time and use but I want a 3rd set, but the next will be the ER-4P!

IMO, the single best thing about the ER4S is their durability. I've literally owned dozens of earphone sets and all but the Etymotics that I continued to use eventually bit the dust. Usually it was a cord discontinuity most likely very near the plug. I've replaced countless cables and plugs, pulling out my soldering iron and rummaging through my collection of parts. Once I got the Etymotics I had put all that behind me. Not once have I had a problem with the ER4S cables or plugs. The only times I have experienced cutout of a channel was when a filter got clogged, which has happened a few times. It's pretty simple to replace a filter, and they give you extra filters and a tool to remove the old filter. I figure I can probably clean the old filters but haven't bothered trying because I have an ample supply of new ones.

I bought the Etymotics because I needed some privacy at my new office job. It wasn't just that I wanted my space, I had a lot of thinking to do and needed to block out distracting noise and at times there was far too much of that. I did some research and determined that the Etymotics were a likely good choice. They were highly touted by audiophiles and had a reputation for being very effective in noisy environments. Of course, they still enjoy that reputation. I no longer have that office job and I mostly use the Etymotics in the gym, where their isolation is just as critical as at that office job.

When I read the reviews before buying my first ER4S I quickly realized that people who used them with portable devices seemed to always use headphone amps, and I assumed that I too would need one and so I bought an Airhead "Headphone Amplifier and Audio Image Processor" at the same time. However, to my amazement and delight I found that I got adequate volume from my portable devices without having to use it. I did use the amp when listening to audio files at my computer, at least sometimes, but have ever since just set aside the Airhead. I have used the ER4S phones without an amplifier with satisfactory results with a Sony WM-FX465 cassette/TV/FM/AM portable, iRiver SlimX IMP-350 portables, iRiver H120 and H140 portables and Sansa Sandisk M250 MP3/FM portables (2 different firmware/chipset models).

My hearing isn't the best, and I won't get into subtle discussions concerning performance in various frequency ranges. However, I recently acquired a set of Sennheiser CX300B earbud headphones and determined that the Etymotics sound far superior. I also don't expect that the Sennheisers are very durable. Also, they came with only one set of buds that fit my ears. The Etymotics came with several sets of both types of buds (the white plastic, which I always use and the foam). I bought extra white plastic tips, but have only had to replace a couple (they got a bit loose over time and would remain in my ear after pulling out the drivers).

It is true that the sound from brushing the cable goes right to your ears and it's a major annoyance. I rarely notice that now, having developed strategies to avoid brushing the cables. I'll take the durability over other considerations!

Lately, I use the ER4S with small Sandisk MP3 players, the M250's. There are 4 different types of M250's and 2 of mine aren't as loud as the 3rd at maximum volume and I've had problems achieving satisfactory listening levels with them at times when using the ER4S's so I anticipate getting the more efficient ER-4P for my 3rd set of Etymotics at some point. I've been reading reviews and considered getting another brand, but I think I'd probably regret that and plan to stick with Etymotic. Fortunately, the price has come down from the $269 + shipping I paid for my last set!

My hearing isn't the best, and I won't get into subtle discussions concerning performance in various frequency ranges. However, I recently acquired a set of Sennheiser CX300B earbud headphones and determined that the Etymotics sound far superior. I also don't expect that the Sennheisers are very durable. Also, they came with only one set of buds that fit my ears. The Etymotics came with several sets of both types of buds (the white plastic, which I always use and the foam). I bought extra white plastic tips, but have only had to replace a couple (they got a bit loose over time and would remain in my ear after pulling out the drivers).

It is true that the sound from brushing the cable goes right to your ears and it's a major annoyance. I rarely notice that now, having developed strategies to avoid brushing the cables. I'll take the durability over other considerations!

I have used the ER4S with small Sandisk MP3 players, the M250's. There are 4 different types of M250's and 2 of mine aren't as loud as the 3rd at maximum volume and I've had problems achieving satisfactory listening levels with them at times when using the ER4S's so I anticipate getting the more efficient ER-4P for my 3rd set of Etymotics at some point. I've been reading reviews and considered getting another brand, but I think I'd probably regret that and plan to stick with Etymotic. Fortunately, the price has come down from the $269 + shipping I paid for my last set!

I also use the ER4S for audio when I watch movies in my home theater. The fidelity is much superior to my AV receiver plus 5.1 speaker system, which is very decent equipment BTW. My comprehension of conversation is much better, and I also don't have to be concerned with disturbing my neighbors.

title: Real Review - Quantified by Examples & Comparisons...
text:
If you are like me, you are struggling through the various reviews to divine what the review considers great sound and how these compare to the real world (versus a recording engineer loving their URI's all mid-range.) In most cars, I would configure the audio system (on a -5 to +5 system) Treble +5, Mid 0 to -5, and Bass +5. I believe at low volume, a system should give you the dynamics of sitting in front of an orchestra, not just acoustic guitar and voice. I use a 5th Generation iPod, and with these ear phones, the LOUDNESS EQ setting. (My past phones on this unit: Original, Bose in-ear, Tri-Ports & Quiet Comfort2.) I like (and have) pretty much all music but country, opera and gangsta.

Addressing the concerns I had when reading the reviews:

Bass.

Yes, these do not compare to Bose's in-ear and tri-ports for booming bass. However, the treble response and crispness do rival the Bose . First you must carefully follow insertion instructions. Then, the Bass is there, however it is very, very accurate and tight. It also requires some volume to bring it out. Throw on some Techmaster PEB and it will render the speaker blowing sub-bass perfectly (this killed my original iPod units.) Have the volume below 50% on Lady Gaga / Beyonce's Telephone, and you will not hear any bass presence. 75% volume and you hear the bass, perfectly and as it was meant to be heard.

In fact, below 50% volume on anything and you do not really hear the bass. This is also because the treble and mid-range performance is amazing and drowns it out. If you are like me and do not like a lot of Mid-Range, you must use the LOUDNESS EQ setting, or the mid-range can bring a headache on.

Volume.

The P versions do not suffer the power issues Bose QC2's do, and better the Tri-Ports and in-ears for ability to pump volume cleanly. You can almost max out every song and feel like you're in a South Beach club with you head next to an amp with an iPod's power. The sweet spot is 60% to 90%. I could also spot the iTunes Plus songs I bought versus the CD's I ripped by compression issues of the iTunes music. These things have a clarity that is truly amazing.

Comfort & Fit.

They fit well when you follow the instructions, but they take a bit to get out of your ears, and it can hurt if you rush it. While I like to throw them on while brushing my teeth in the morning, these are not quick on quick off things. You must remove one side to take a phone call, they do block. Also, like any ear plug, they feel a bit unnatural to me, and the absence of ambient noise feels strange. The "rustling" of the cables has not bothered me much yet, but they do make it thump, so I guess if you jog with them it might get irritating. PS: No matter how clean you think your ears are, have a napkin ready when you take these out.

Conclusion:

I do not know about the wire's longevity (my last Bose In-Ears died from cable failure) and that is my biggest concern. However, I do think they are better than the Bose offerings, the price and discomfort of them being paid back and then some in clarity and accuracy of sound. Really, you will not believe an iPod is capable of this quality.

title: Accurate monitors for sure.  Highly Recommend.
text:
Hello all, I purchased a set of Etymotic ER-4Ps around a month ago. ( September 2009 ) I have listened to a wide variety of music from a few different sources. Primary music focus for very critical listening: Movie scores/Classical/Jazz/Psy-Trance. Sources include PC/Laptop/iPhone/Amplifier.

These in ear monitors allow a lot of details to come through. They do a nice job of isolating ambient noise. They will also let you hear every single tick and crackle in a cheap PC integrated sound card. On a nicer PC sound card or real amplifier they sound great. They are efficient enough to play very well from an iPhone. ( I need to use an adapter as they will not fit direct to first gen iPhone )

I have listened to the James Horner score to Sneakers countless times since the score was released. I know its details better than any other album. It is my own reference point. In my home stereo setup when I upgraded my speakers to some Cambridge Soundworks T200 full towers. I was so amazed at the details I never heard before. Shocked in fact that I have never made them out before. The same level of shock was realized with the ER-4Ps. I am hearing yet again, more details I have never ever noticed before on the Sneakers soundtrack. Specifically an upright bass recorded at very low levels in the background of several tracks. They are deep in the background and until I heard the score on the ER-4Ps I never it was there in as many places as it is. This experience is repeating with many albums. I am going through all my favorite albums anticipating hearing things I always missed. That is exciting. For that reason alone I recommend these highly.

The point is these IEMs ( In Ear Monitors ) play what you give them. They do not mask, enhance or change the sound at all. I used a freeware utility ( sinegen.exe ) to do some tone generator tests. The ER-4Ps trail off rapidly between 16.5khz and 17 khz. This is really not going to be noticeable in a track. I am comparing to a 15 year old pair of Denon Over the Ear-phones who have served me well up to this point. The Denons ( on the same source PC ) trailed off very gradually but audio could be heard to about 22k with volume levels set way up. The ER-4Ps trail off to 0 by 17.5-18k regardless of amplification levels. Again let me be clear that I am hearing clarity and definition much greater in the ER-4Ps than the Denons.

Working my way through the sound level spectrum output is consistent and linear, read: very flat, way far down. You can hear a sine wave generation down to 25 hz. Levels trail off to 0 below that. It seems that the correct levels of energy are reproduced through a very wide range.

Let me be clear, the CORRECT level is produced. These do not over-boom-ify like most in ear cannons are expected to do to provide brain massages. IF there is heavy bass recorded, you WILL hear it. If the recording was made ( often ) to anticipate a system with the bass turned up to eleventy-seven, you will not hear much deep bass.

You will hear the music, as it is recorded. They are clearly monitors. They may not be for everyone who wants purely entertainment in a casual environment. If you appreciate accuracy and fidelity and expect to hear so many details of a track, these ARE the IEMs for you.

They do a very nice job of muting outside noise. I have been able to wrap the cords over my ears, forward then over and around the back to all but eliminate the microphone effect. The clip provided also helps with that. Without wrapping or clipping the cables will pick up a lot of noise. Ambient in-the-air noise is cut way down.

In the office I work in, there is steady hum of air conditioning , the lite-fm over the PA, and in the computer data center, deafening cooling and equipment noise. Wearing these nulls out those sounds very well. Better than foam insert ear plugs, with no audio even playing. With a track playing you are in your own sonic universe. Really amazing.

They are great in a library too. You can have them on at standard listening levels and the person sitting next to you will not hear them. The apple ear buds waste so much sound ( and people play them so loud ) that I can usually make out words from 20 foot away from some listeners. It bothers me, and it must indicate severe hearing damage to the poor listener. Not a problem with the ER-4Ps. You and you alone hear all the music and only the music through the ER-4Ps.

You do not need to play these loud at all to hear everything. They handle high volumes nicely tho. Be careful tho, you could will likely do damage to your ears turning these up to full power.

The ER-4Ps take a few seconds each ear to seat correctly. I have not had the troubles that others have had. My ears happen to fit fine with the standard smaller mushroom cap inserts. You will know you have a good fit when outside noise drops to about 5% normal. I gave them 4 stars for comfort because after an hour or so it feels like its time to take them out and let your ears breath and stretch a bit. That may be the case with all in-ears.

I got a chance to listen to some V-Modas that my cousin got last year. They were 1/2 the price as the ER-4Ps. They were not as accurate, but definitely more "fun". I would recommend V-Modas ( not sure the model but they go for around $80) for casual listeners who want big booms. They are a bit easier to insert and take out.

I waited over a month to write a review. I did not want to give a pre-mature/just-spent-the-cash-and-now-I-must-justify-it/fan-boy review.

Edit: One possible downside, the cabling is very fine. I am very careful with them always. It feels like you *need* to be careful with them. For transport the kit does come with a larger hard case and small soft zipper pouch. The low mass of the earpiece and cabling makes them effectively weightless in your ears.

I am truly enjoying them. And listening to them for a few hours a day at work without fatigue.

Update: July 2010.
I still love them! They are holding up perfectly, sound great, and I would still recommend them.

Update: December 2015
Still using them basically every day at work. Good stuff.
Their accuracy will expose weaknesses in your source. These sounded amazing on the LG G2. But kinda meh on the LG G4. Looking into an external DAC/Amp.

Update: January 2016
Oh noes! I just had my first indication of the cabling finally letting go. One channel is dropping out depending on how the cable is moved. Replacement cables are available from $35 to $200+. When I replace the cables it will be of the cheaper variety. I might attempt to replace the bad portion of the cable and DIY a patch.

Daniel

title: If you just can't wear earphones, then get these.
text:
My earphones always fall out. Nothing fits. Total nightmare. I hate using speakerphone (worse than the voice quality at drive-ins) and refuse to fry my brain by holding my cellphone to my ear. (The research is in folks, cellphones are very bad for your brain, so keep your phone away from you!)
These earphones stay in and are comfortable. Not super duper pillow soft comfy, but pretty darn good. And the sound quality is great.
A lot of people don't like the flat cord, but I don't have a problem with it. Treat it with care and it will last.
After heating them, don't touch them on anything or they'll stick like glue and you'll have a mess.
Touch to your ear, and if too hot, then wait another 10 seconds.
Press in ear VERY firmly, and let cool in ear. If you do this, then you'll get a perfect fit first time.
Let dry for a couple hours before trying to use them.
Get a FawkesBOX and put your phone in there while not using. I only use the inner copper sleeve, not the outer metal tin. The sleeve blocks almost all the radiation, and you can still get messages.

title: The Jabra wireless running headphones are quite awesome and a great first iteration of the product
text:
The Jabra wireless running headphones are quite awesome and a great first iteration of the product.

What Works :
1. Ran on 5k, 10k runs on both paved tracks, semi-paved running trails, in variety of conditions like hot humid, cool early morning, in North Carolina, as well as when went to Washington DC, and the ear buds never fell down. It's a strange feeling, sometimes I felt they are loose and will come off, but they don't! I am using the default medium sized covers on them and the medium gel ear covering.
2. Sound is really awesome. It feels like an orchestra in the ears. Especially at a bit of a medium to high volume, you get immersive sound. Better than my BeatsX in overall sound experience for me. If you are in heavy Bass, these ones are not too "bassy" so heavy hip hop or bass sounds may sound less heavy, but overall sound experience for me was totally much better than all my other headphones which I have quite a few.
3. The charging case is top quality and you simply store the buds in them, and it keeps them charged, as long as of course you keep the case charged with its supplied USB cord.
4. The headphones battery is very powerful and I have had multiple 5k runs with no charging needed. They advertise 4.5 hours in one shot and the case can charge them further. I am not a marathon runner, for me the 4.5 hours itself is more than enough.
5. You get liberated when you run - it's just you, the open track, the wind in your face, and the music. This is big. These headphones don't come into the way of your running experience. Earlier I used the wireless Beats X and I felt the cord bothering me on my neck. These are truly seamless. The first one time you will feel they are bulky, but once you get used to them, which for me was the second time itself, now I don't even realize I am wearing them.
6. The heart rate is detected pretty fast and accurately, and is a very useful feature to have.
7. The headphones integrate as a device with various popular running apps like Runkeeper. These apps recognize the headphones as a bluetooth device that is tracking heart rate, as well as can play music playlists. These apps are also able to write onto Healthkit information used by my apple iPhone and apple Watch.
8. The quality of material is robust. the headphones once fell down by me on the pavement, and nothing happened, they sound and work great.
9. You can use only the right headphone if you want in one ear.
10. You can use the app to locate the headphones if you can't find them.
11. The controls are on the headphones to control volume, pause etc.
12. They work seamlessly well in sweat and light rain, I have experienced. The water/sweat proof rating is correct, and they don't fall of or have any difference in sound or any material issues with the heavy use by me in sweat and running.
13. Works well as a hands free device, with great sound quality and all expected controls to mute, volume all working fine.
14. They come with 3 types of wing tips, 3 types of gel ear bud coverings and 3 types of black silicon ear bud coverings, so you can try your best fit.

What needs improvement in next iteration of product :
1. The bass can be a bit more heavier to compete with products like BeatsX which are also quite tiny but provide better bass.
2. The headphone controls to control volume, pause, play are a bit less polished than I would like, it should be more easy to just tap lightly or scroll your finger (touch sensitive) to make it work. I still could not figure out the voice pass through feature wherein you can hear the ambient noise of environment around you by double tapping your headphone in addition to the music. Controls can be better in next iteration.
3. The native app of Jabra does not write to health kit directly, so in order for activities to register to my apple watch and phone Health app, I have to use apps like Runkeeper. This reduces the need to use the native Jabra app.

General notes :
1. The price point currently is 249 as of writing, they need to bring it down to below 199 for sure eventually, in order to be more attractive. I am pretty sure eventually it will happen.
2. These are not goofy looking like Apple AirPods, and they look urban cool with its black matte color really accentuating the runner's spirit.

title: These honestly might be the best headphones I've ever had
text:
These honestly might be the best headphones I've ever had. I've used them heavily for six months and they've yet to disappoint. They sound fantastic, they pair easily, and the recharging case is a huge plus. Previously, I had Bose Sound Sports which just wouldn't stay in my ear.

I will note, the fins that came with them made it tough to get a good fit. I ended up shortening the medium incrementally with a lighter. I kept trying it out until the fit was right. Now it fits in my ear like a glove.

title: A bit bulky, but great for music, movies, health monitoring
text:
Technology has come such a long way. I thought these would be good to use as stereo buds for music from my Kindle, phone etc. But, what is really neat is the fact that you can use it to monitor your heart rate from your phone. This is amazing. Without the need for an arm band monitor. The set comes with a case that actually is used to charge the buds. You can charge up to two times on a single charge. This is great. Next, is that you install the Jabra Sport app on your phone and when paired it monitors your heart rate and takes you through many tests to assess your health.

It comes with 2 sets of 3 of buds and 3 sets of ear wings. The buds are gel or foam. I like the memory foam because you get better base and also isolation. I also tested these through my Amazon Fire Stick. I paired them, turned on a show on Hulu and was able to hear amazing sound.

The part I kind don't like, is that the buds themselves take a bit to get used to. Even though they are foam, they are a bit foam and afterwards, kind of hurt. I wear ear buds for playing drums and the ones I use are fully isolation but they are softer and don't fatigue the ear canal as much as these. The ear wings get tucked inside the ear for a snug fit and it also is used to connect to your heart rhythm.

The other feature these have is that if you use the isolation foam, you can double tap a button and you can actually hear what's around you. This is pretty cool. It has full volume control and you can start an app from a press of a button as well.

Full of features. Again, you need to ensure you got the right fit, otherwise you'll fatigue pretty quickly.

title: Insane value headphones. Sold my B&O H4 for these.
text: I had a pair of B&O H4 that weren't bad, but I bought these as a second set and my dad and I, whom are somewhat audiophiles, did back to back testing. They were near even - if anything an edge to the Sony. The difference? You can pick these up for $100-150 and the B&O were in the $350 range. Anyways - apples to oranges. Noise cancelling is very good. Not the best outdoors especially with wind or at the gym if you walk past an industrial size fan. The bluetooth connection can get funky in very cold weather for some reason too (I set to best effort vs best quality to help). Comfort is amazing, design is very good and hasn't aged in my opinion. They're significantly heavier than the XM3 or XM4, but if I'm not comparing them to anything, I've never felt like they were too heavy or uncomfortable. If I wear them for hours straight while being active, my ears will start to get warm, but that's hardly a complaint. Battery life is insane. I use them regularly and can get maybe a month out of them before needing a charge. The touch features for volume and song skip work well. Sometimes I fumble with the more complicated motions. Some people have complained about the swivel hinges breaking. I was very concerned about this. I bought mine refurbished and have used them a couple years or so at home, at work, and throw them in a cheap $10 case in my bag to go to the gym and the hinges are perfectly fine. You could nit pick them all day, but at the end of the day, they sound phenomenal especially for the price range.

The side touch feature is my favorite part, though. Being able to skip a song, go replay one, pause/play and answer calls on the fly is fantastic. The overall sound quality is great, the ability to use the Sony app to play with the equalizer is also fun. Ambient sound is great for listening to music and holding a conversation, and the microphone seems to work good for calls as I haven't had anyone complain about voice quality yet. Overall I'd give these an amazing rating and would suggest them for around the $100 range without a seconds thought.

title: I do not recommend these earbuds.  They have a serious design flaw.
text:
I would have easily given these earbuds 4 or 5 stars, if it wasn't for the "low battery" warning. JLAB clearly put no thought into this. Here are my issues:

1) The first low battery warning occurs about 5 minutes before the battery dies . So if you just started your jog, or just got on the bus, you're screwed. With 6 hours of play time, the low battery notification should give you at least 20 minutes notice. Since you are almost always "out and about" when listening to headphones, it would be nice to have enough juice to finish your activity or get where you are going.

2) The low battery message (which is verbal) repeats FREQUENTLY for the brief remainder of your battery life, constantly interrupting your music. This is so annoying you wind up taking the earbuds off.

Since the earbuds are essentially useless once you get the first low battery warning, the warning serves no purpose. Giving the low battery warnings at the 30, 20 and 10 minute marks would be far less annoying and actually give you a chance to get to a charger.

Cons: Reset was difficult when suddenly failing to connect properly after 2 days of use, nearly returned it.
•Lack of accurate sound quality could exacerbate noise processing disorders if used as the only device long term. But reasonable for audiobooks and phone calls.

Pros: I LOVE neck style leashed buds, the flexiband is more stable than expected when at work.

No ANC in-ear plugs I've used (Including Bose) block all sounds. That's not how ANC works. You need over ear plus ANC for industrial use.

title: Not sound-proof, but good enough for office use.
text:
I knew right away that these would be my office headphones. I have a mechanical keyboard that I use at work, and the office I work in is semi-open. There's a *lot* of noise coming every-which-way. These are a much-needed accessory to my work productivity, as I'm easily distracted by things in my periphery, whether visually or auditory.

The presentation is great. The box is very high quality, reminiscent of the recent Samsung Galaxy device boxes. A smooth matte feel with gloss--weirdly pristine. The box slides out of the slipcover and you get the headphones already in the case. What I like is that they're folded, and there's even a little sheet underneath the phones that always reminds you how to put them back in. Also included is a 3.5mm cable in case you don't want to use Bluetooth, a charging cable, and an adapter. The case is nice, but as I keep mine at work I can't testify to its durability. There's a thin mesh net on the backside in case anyone needs to store one or two thin headphone accessory/-ies along. The accent colors are a nice light copper/rose gold color. I love that color; I'm glad it's getting more attention in recent years.

It didn't take long to charge the headphones, so they come with a little bit of juice. As soon as you turn them on, you get a soft beep along with a voice indicating they're turned on. Nice responsive feedback. Once I put them on I could hear the headphones working to drown out the sound; there was a thick veil of soundproofing that was draped over my ears as soon as the earpads touched them.

The first thing I did was listen to podcasts through the Pocket Casts app and .flac music through Poweramp v3. With podcasts, the difference was phenomenal. Listening to "Wait, wait... Don't tell me!" made me feel as though I were in the audience. The music was fantastic...until I tried on my other headphones which I use for music only.
I thought the bass might've been too strong with the Sony headphones, and I was right. After using even "cheaper" headphones like the Audio-Technica M50x, I could tell the Sony had too much bass. I'm not sure if that's partly because of the noise-canceling technology or what, but the bass can be toned down a bit, methinks.

I then proceeded to download the supplementary app to get the fullest suite of attributes the headphones can get. The app works well, and I didn't experience any hiccups while actually using the app. The only hiccup was when I was trying to download the update. It took *forever*. Almost an hour and it was just halfway through. I decided to bring them to work the next day and let the app sit there while updating. Thankfully, it remembers the progress, even though the app kept crashing during the update process.

There are some optimization tweaks in the app, some sound profiles to let you configure the noise cancelation level (yes, level; the noise cancelation is pure software; you can set it to drown out the most noise as possible or have no noise cancellation at all), and even a little snippet of what is currently playing through the headphones. A simple UI with all the features you need.

The first few days I used it I was active, and I kept noticing that my ears sometimes would pop depending on whether I sat down or arose quickly. Another weird thing is that when I take the headphones off, my ears sometimes need a minute or two to adjust. There's so much noise in the world! After taking the headphones off I can hear HVAC activity and my loud work neighbor who's otherwise not that loud.

I had some headphones with some touch controls before and always found them tacky. I used them once when I first got them and never again. But with these headphones, I'm always using the tap gesture to play/pause and the swipe gesture to raise or lower the volume. There are also swipe gestures to skip or go back a track, but since I never do that anyway I never use those gestures. You have to be careful with the tap; when it works, it works. But the whole surface isn't the active portion and you have to hit it right in the center. Sometimes I'm hitting my finger against my ears trying to find the spot and hurting myself in the process. I tested the gesture where you put your entire palm on the cup to turn off the noise canceling feature and let the mic allow incoming conversation, but not after the third try. I could hear the other people just fine, but I found the right hand over my ear felt awkward, and one person didn't realize I could even hear them. Putting your hand over your headphones isn't a gesture people immediately see as you paying attention to them.

The headphones are extremely lightweight and comfortable to use; I left them on for about two hours once before having to take them off. I actually was surprised with how light they were; when I got the Amazon box I didn't believe it was my headphones. It was much lighter than expected.

For my first noise-canceling headphones I'm pleased. The sound balance can be better (less bass), but they make for fantastic headphones to use at work. I wasn't sure what I was expecting with noise-canceling technology. I thought it would drown out all noises, but you still can hear the occasional mutter; it just won't be distinct.

Oh, forgot to mention the battery life. I charged it only once and have been using it for a week, at about an hour or two each day. Still going well. If you press the power button once it will tell you the battery level. AFter the initial update the voice indicator might give the wrong battery level (it did for me), but give it about ten or fifteen minutes to adjust and it will go back to normal.

title: Excellent sound, frustrating bluetooth and terrible mic
text:
Sound and noise canceling are best-of-breed, if that's all you need: this is a pretty good buy. Comfortable, charges quickly, battery lasts, and the touch control is actually fairly nice. Especially the "cover an ear to hear the outside world" "gesture", that's a stroke of brilliance.

If you want to hook up to more than one device at a time though, it's a surprisingly painful experience. Generally speaking it only connects to one thing at a time, and *does not accept connections from other devices*. So if you want to switch from your phone to your computer, you need to explicitly disconnect from the phone, then connect from the computer. And do the reverse to go back (it'll happily reconnect to your now-sleeping laptop, and will refuse to switch to your phone).
It also has a bad habit of either being (much) too quiet or (somewhat) too loud, with no volume steps in between. My phone volume is only at 20% or 30% while listening to music, and I need to go into an EQ to turn down everything so 30% isn't uncomfortably loud. And I've needed to do that for everything I've connected it to. On a PC it's fine since there's much finer-grained volume control, but wow. Frustrating.

It feels like I'm dealing with a bluetooth device from 10 years ago. Shockingly bad, especially since it's clearly software issues that could be fixed (but haven't, a full year after launch). Coupled with a $300 price tag and it's simply inexcusable.

The microphone has been covered at length on youtube - do yourself a favor and listen to to the examples. In a quiet environment it sounds like you're speaking from another room, and anywhere louder it's almost unusable. The microphone is bad enough that I'm very strongly considering returning it and getting a Bose instead, it might as well not exist.

title: Amazing ANC
text:
When I was first thinking about writing a review for this product, I was going to start picking apart the sound quality.
Then I realized, is it really fair to compare these to open-back audiophile headphones that cost four times what these do?
The answer is no. That's not what you're getting here, and that's not what these are meant to be.
These headphones (and headphones like these) have a specific use case, and it is not critical listening.
So instead, I'll review based on that use case.

The noise cancellation on these things is outstanding!
I'm typing this on a mechanical keyboard right now, and I only hear music.
To be fair, I have spent very little time listening to Bose headphones, so I would not be the best person for a direct comparison.
What I can say for sure, however, is that these work really well.

A couple of negative points:

They could be a little more comfortable for someone with a head and ears the size of mine, but I'm used to that by now.
The bass is very present, but it's a bit loose and sloppy (not tight or accurate), and mids take a definite back seat.
It is very easy to accidentally change tracks when trying to adjust the cans.

These things being mentioned, these headphones are good enough at what they do (in context of what they are meant for - private listening, airplane listening, etc.) to be worthy of a five-star review.
If there are better ANC headphones out there, I have never tried them.

I will say though that they are VERY comfortable, easily adjustable for fit, and I like the 'desert' color which differentiates it from the typical black headphone. text:

The build quality of this stand is bar none. The stand comes packaged in a flat black box and all the pieces are encased in styrofoam casing. This is one solid and heavy stand that is well balanced and no fear of it tipping over. You have to put the stand together as it comes in 3 pieces base, neck, and hanger. The hardware is 4 small screws and metal plate that attaches the neck to the hanger stand underneath. The neck attaches to the base with 2 longer screws that you screw in from underneath the stand. There are 3 rubber foot pads attached and one that you attach after screwing the base to the neck.

This is high grade aluminum with attention paid to detail and design. I didn't experience any sharp edges per say, the cuts are all beveled but I can see how some people may think that by the angles on the hanger. The finish is a matte feel of which i have no issues, I like it because once you place your cans on it they stay rock solid in place. It fits my Sennheiser Momentums 2.0 Wireless and Oppo PM-3 with plenty of room underneath them.

The only drawback and it is a minor one is that the stand provides no type of cable management.You either detach the cable of or you can wrap around the neck (ugly look).

title: Not quite as good as the Bose QC35
text:
These are perfectly good headphones, but since they're a copycat product they have to be judged in comparison to the product they're copying (Bose QC35).

-Noise cancelling - Winner Sony. The Bose are really good but I think the Sony's are noticeably better.
- Sound quality - tie - both are very good
- Bluetooth range - Winner Sony - The Sony's have a slightly more stable connection in worst-case conditions (when running a microwave nearby which is across the house from the Bluetooth connection, the Bose drop out more than the Sony's do.)
- Connectivity - Winner Bose - The Bose can connect to 2 devices, they honestly don't work super well (sometimes it's not clear which ones are connected or there's some bugginess). But at least Bose is trying - Sony's only connect to one device... to switch devices you have to turn off the bluetooth on the device and manually connect to the other device which is a PITA.
- Interface - Winner Bose - Lot of minor stuff. Bose has really good voice synthesis, and can pronounce your computer name. For example, I named my computer "The Mattbook Pro", and the Bose successfully pronounces it: "Connected to... the Mattbook pro". Obviously the voice isn't preprogrammed, and it's voice synthesis is surprisingly good. The Sony is okay but it just has per-recorded voice clips so it can't say the name of the device it's connected to. Next, the play/pause on the Sony is okay, and I think the touchpad gestures are pretty good/logical. But they're inconsistent, sometimes the play/pause double tap doesn't register, sometimes the track forward gesture registers as volume down, etc., etc. The discrete buttons on the Bose are better, although they're not perfect either, there's double tapping, triple tapping, etc, to control track fw/back, which are annoying to execute.
- Comfort - Winner Bose - The Bose earcups are a little comfier in my opinion.
- Appearance - Winner Bose - The Sony's are unnecessarily large, I think the Bose look a little nicer. The Sony's stick out farther than necessary.
- Charging - Winner Sony - The Sony charges via USB-C which is nicer and more future-proof than micro USB the Bose uses. But it's not that big of a deal.

Anyway, I was originally skeptical of bluetooth headsets due to their price, but if you don't have a pair I'd highly recommend buying a pair. Both the Sony's and the Bose ones are pretty good, so just get whichever one you like the best.

title: Good at what they do, but didn't last
text:
I am writing this review on the day the headphones died. 61 days after I got them. I was very careful with them, but they mysteriously died on my desk in the night. This fact is the most important part of the review.
Aside from that terrible, fatal flaw I really liked them though. For listening to podcasts and audio books while working out they were great. You can hear the media fine, but also hear the world well enough to not get hit by a bus or anything. Battery life was great. Like maybe almost 12 hours. But none of this justifies them dying in only 2 months.
A few downsides: because of their shape the only way to safely transport them is on your head. There's just no good way to pack them. Also, any pure tones are waaaay louder than anything else. So if you are listening to something at a comfortable volume on your phone and some kind of notification comes through and makes a beeping noise it will rattle your skull. I don't know why and no amount of tweaking setting on my phone fixed it.
Several reviews say they cant be adjusted. Those people are wrong. The part holding the left and right ear pieces together is a piece of stiff wire. You bend it to adjust the fit of the headphones.
Some people are saying these aren't bone conduction headphones but just tiny blutooth speakers. I don't know what they are expecting but its true that you can hear the headphones when they are off your head. The inducers aren't some magic device that will vibrate your skull but not the air. But when you put them on they sound like normal headphones because those vibrations are going into your head and not the air. People around you cant hear them unless they are turned up way too loud. Just like normal headphones.

title: If you have to wear headphones for work, try these.
text:
I moved from the Plantronics to the Sennheiser and so far, it's been a win for me. The primary difference between the Plantronics and the Sennheiser is the lack of the weak link on the cord. Where the cord plugs into the dongle went intermittent on two Plantronics headsets.

The Sennheiser avoids this by eliminating the cord. The headset can connect via BT to the phone and via a USB dongle in my laptop to the computer. This eliminates the weak point but means the headset is not charging while in use. That problem is basically eliminated by the super super super fast charging on the stand. I can plug the headset into the stand for 15 or 20 minutes and get a full day's use out of it.

I'm pretty much not finding anything concerning about the Sennheiser. You do have to pop off a piece of the earphone on the mic side to perform updates but that's not really a problem. Also, I'm a bit clumsy and getting the headset over the stand can be challenging to people like me that refuse to use two hands. Neither of these are concerning.

text:

My intended uses for the headset are the following: (1) Business calls at my desk in my home office, (2) Conference calls in my car when there's a lot of traffic noise, (3) Music when I'm out walking---with an occasional business call interruption.

This headset is excellent for the following reasons:

• The conversation sound quality---on both ends of the call---is excellent. Crisp and clear---especially consonants.
• Music quality is very good.
• Easy to set up and sync with my smart phone
• Comfortable to wear for prolonged periods
• Speaker on both ears makes it easier to hear and concentrate on a call in a noisy car
• Controls are easy to use: answer, hang up, mute, un-mute, volume up and down, Room Experience.
• Easy to charge

If you rely on a headset for clear communication, this headset is definitely worth the price.

To protect the headset, I ordered a protective case: [[ASIN:B00LB07HZY Sennheiser Carrying Case for Headset - Black 506059]]

title: Finally - They stay on my ears and sound good
text:
I have had way too many sets of headphones. Mostly because my dog eats them if they are within reach. While I still have not found the perfect headset with these, they come pretty close.

Durability and battery Life - Way too early to tell. I'll update this after a few months.

Noise Canceling- Let’s get something straight - if you put your fingers in your ears, they will cancel noise. That's called passive noise canceling, or simply, blocking outside noise. True active noise canceling head phones are over the ear, and usually very expensive. These head phones do a pretty good job passively blocking outside noise by fitting very well to the ear and being angled correctly.

Sound - Everyone has different tastes when it comes to what they like to hear. Some headphones have good or bad ranges from high to low. But it is the quality of the range that matters. For instance, I like to hear bass, and to me there is nothing worse than a tinny am radio sound. These definitely have bass, but it's a bit muddy. The good news is I was able to adjust the equalizer on my phone to clean it up, mostly. Overall all though, for the price, the sound quality is pretty darn good.

Fit & Hold - They Fit and stay put! The best part of these headphones is they fit my ears perfectly. The part that goes around the ear has a wire going through it, unlike so many others. This allows you to mold the over ear wires exactly to you ear and they do not fall out. None of the last several sets I had do this, and it is an enormous benefit.

Controls - The are typical up and down volume and a center button that is used for on, off, hold, answer, etc. I wish the volume buttons were reversed, but that's just being picky. They announce power on, power off and connected. Sadly, they do not announce battery life.

Appearance – Meh. They are a bit big and boxy, but I don’t know how that‘s different from having white things hanging out of your ears for $200.00

Overall - I am giving this 5 starts not because they are the best headphones. I am giving them 5 starts because they check off almost all of my boxes and the price it great. So, 5 stars for overall function and price.

Note: I paid full price for these and I was not asked to review them. Also, if you like this review, please indicate so below. Thanks.

text:
Normally I use big and bulky over ear noise cancelling headphones when sitting at the computer, but obviously that's not as much of a solution when you're standing in line at the store or want music for monotonous tasks like cleaning. In those cases, a pair of ear buds comes in handy, but not all of them are created equal as I discovered with my previous pair.

I like to put on Ihsahn's Arktis album while I do the dishes, but I need to keep an ear out to make sure the toddler isn't up to no good (spoiler alert: he probably is). Unfortunately my old pair didn't wrap around the ear, so I had to have one dangling free that was always getting in my way or getting stuck on the lip of the counter top.

These wrap-around buds from Mucro are much more helpful, since I can keep the secondary bud wrapped around my ear but not actually inserted into my ear canal, meaning I can still hear what's going on through that ear.

The buds themselves swivel around in different positions for maximum comfort to fit any ear size. While that's a pro rather than a con, there is a downside to note. The fact that I'm into avant-garde Norwegian black metal should have told you I have long hair, and it swishes around. title: They do what they say they do!
text:
Overall, these seem to be very good earbuds. Here are the things I liked and didn't like.

Likes

- I love the idea of a case. My earbuds are either thrown in my purse, my gym bag, or in a drawer. They get banged up, the rubber covers get lost, they are always tangled, etc. Having a nice little case to put them in before they go into my purse/gym bag/drawer is fantastic!

- They seem to cancel out noise pretty well and have an overall good sound.

- The six sizes of covers should easily fit anyone's ear, even if you have very small/large ear canals or odd shaped ones. Not to mention, it is nice to have backups if you forget your case and lose them in your purse/gym bag/drawer! :)

- I don't use the microphone, but that is a benefit none of my other earbuds have. If you are a microphone user, having this option along with a high quality set of earbuds would be very nice.

Dislikes

- Price - Up until now, I have been using Skull Candy Inkd earbuds. The sound quality is the same, the noise canceling is pretty much the same, and the rubber covers are identical (granted, there are only 3 vs the 6 here). I can buy these for under $10 if I watch for a sale. The Logitech ones are $80. That is a BIG difference. Obviously, if you used the microphone, the Skull Candy isn't going to work for you though.

So, my final thoughts are that they are very good earbuds and if you need a microphone or have difficulties finding earbuds that are comfortable in your ears, definitely give the Logitech ones a shot. If you are like me and don't use the microphone and don't have fit issues, there are much cheaper alternatives that are just as good.

UPDATE:

I have been using these for about six months in the gym and had to come back and update my review. I hate them. They don't do a good job of canceling noise at all. I can have my music turned up and can still hear everyone talking around me, the noise from equiptment being used, etc. Also, the ear buds don't stay in place and want to fall out of my ears. I have the same size rubber things on them as I do on my other ear buds and those stay in perfectly. With these, I'm constantly shoving them tighter in my ears and then when I take them out, sometimes the rubber part comes off and I have to dig it out of my ear canal which is somewhat scary. The case I loved to protect them has also been a disappointment. The back hinge broke after maybe 50 openings making it useless. The only good thing I can say about them is that they don't tangle much.

title: Some Android Functionality
text:
=====================
The Pros
=====================
+ [6 Sizes of Ear Plugs]
5 sizes of the plastic earbuds and 1 set of foam Comply buds.
+ [Some Android Functionality]
Though only officially stated to work with the iPhone/iPad/iPod, the center button of the controller does work on some Android phones. I have a Nexus One and can confirm all the functionality listed for iPhone also works with the N1 (Play/Pause, Answer/Hang-up, Skip)
+ [Basic Protective Case]
It's certainly nothing impressive, but the basic protective case is indeed a hard shell that will protect your earbuds...Though you've got to curl them up fairly snugly to fit into the case. Personally, I use Camel SNUS chewing tobacco tins. They only cost a few bucks, have a nice oval shape and solid protection.
+ [Flat Cable]
As advertised, the wires are flat (and look like black chinese noodles) and tangling is minimal.
+ [Controls on Right-Side Earbud Wire]
The mic is in the controller so, for one, that puts the mic closer to your mouth and a fringe benefit is that it's easy to quickly know which earbud is meant for the right ear (since the controller is on the right wire)
+ [Great Sound]
The bass could be stronger and the vocals can sometimes seem a bit "tinny", but overall these drivers produce rich, clear, detailed sound. I would attribute the sometimes tinny vocals with music to perhaps Logitech tuning these drivers to be more vocals oriented (these are also used for calls afterall).

=====================
The Cons
=====================
Other than the minor quips already stated with the pros, there's really nothing else I can offer in terms of cons.

=====================
Conclusion
=====================
As a comparison I also have the V-Moda Vibe Earbuds, as well as the Logitech Ultimate Ears TripleFi10. The TripleFi10 being the big-big-big Brother of these 500vi buds, it's not fair to compare the two, but I must admit the 500vi did quite well in comparison! As already stated in the pros section, the 500vi could be better in a couple of spots but overall gives a very respectable performance. The V-Moda was my everyday buds as I like their bass output (and the rather large and clunky TripleFi10s are more a once in a while use), but where the V-Moda excels in bass, they're rather weak in clarity and depth.

All that said, these 500vi buds are my new everyday buds, with the bonus of also being a headset for my Nexus One and I have no problem recommending them

title: Great headphones for the money
text:
These are excellent headphones for the money. I use professional in-ear monitors for instrument monitoring and am relatively picky with a preference for a flat and natural audio presentation. I have been displeased with most general in-ear headphones for casual listening but not these.

While the audio presentation isn't what I would call flat it is pretty close. Bass extension is good and clear. No mud or over-extension which covers up the rest of the audio presentation. Very nice mid range and high end detail but I have found the highs a little fatiguing until the drivers break in a bit. Volume level doesn't seem to negatively affect the audio experience and remains proportionate throughout.

There are plenty of ear tips included to ensure a good fit and seal with terrific separation from the environment around you. Assembly quality is sturdy although the included plastic storage case is garbage though and too small to be usable.

title: Excellent value for a kid headphone - WORKS FOR THE PLANE
text:
I had bought a pair of JLab kid headphones for my daughter a year or so ago from Wal Mart for about $15 and they were essentially garbage. The combo of a steep rolloff of high frequencies (I'm guessing around 13Khz) and the volume limiter made them impossible to use for any kind of noisy environment like an airplane or even a car.

...These are a huge upgrade from that AND at a lower price. They have a full frequency response (which allows you to listen at lower volumes due to being able to hear detail) and the 93db volume limit allows for listening in noisy places without risk of hearing damage. They are durable for my 2 & 5 YO. The daisy chain feature is also a great bonus. Now, the overall sound quality isn't going to compare to any serious headphone (obviously) and the background noise isolation could be better but for the $$, it would be tough to find something better.

title: Good quality set of headphones
text:
I've tried several different types of inexpensive-mid range headphones and these are by far my favorite out of all the ones that I've tried. Maybe more importantly though is not that they are "better than other headphones" but rather that as that a stand-alone product they are actually really good. They are made from good quality materials and have a good sound. This is one product that I felt like actually came and looks pretty much exactly like the picture in the product description. They are designed with cushion pretty much everywhere, so your head doesn't get pinched in weird ways that make it hurt. The earpieces (earmuffs?) are comfortable and isolate the sound pretty well. Both what you're listening to from those around you as well as the ambient noise that might bother/distract you. They fold up for storage, and fold up smoothly. Like I said before, I'm impressed. I always try to think of cons and here are my biggest three:

1.) The cable isn't detachable. It's plenty long which gives you a lot of freedom but I wish it were detachable
2.) The color is super bright. I like it a lot most of the time. . . but it definitely makes you stand out which isn't always what I'm going for.
3.) The sound is good but not so good that it blows you away

Overall I really like them and assuming that they continue to work I will definitely continue to recommend them.
I was fortunate enough to be able to review these and get a discount on the price but I give them 5 stars because I am super happy with them and think that they deserve them. I definitely don't give everything 5 stars.

title: Wouldn't pay non-sale price
text:
As a newly invited Vine reviewer, I was tickled pink to be able to review a headphone that might replace the earbuds for my MP3 player. While I received the set for free as long as I reviewed it, I pride myself on being as honest as I can with any review. On that note, while I thought the set was OK, but I wouldn't pay full price for it.

I mainly use headphones to listen to audiobooks in restaurants when I eat on my own, so I was particularly interested in the noise cancelling component of the set. While it didn't completely keep the sound of kids out, it actually worked pretty well for dulling the ambient noise. Of course, I've got to take them off when talking with the restaurant's staff, but that's not a big deal. Since I'm using an MP3 player, I connect them with the included audio wire, which initially didn't play sound in both ears. After fiddling with it, they both came on and I could hear just fine. The Bluetooth hooked up seamlessly with my cell, so there's no issue there. I also like how the left and right ears are very clearly labeled inside the "ear cups", so there's no fumbling around when trying to put them on. Its initial charge was quick, about 2 hours. I haven't run down the battery yet, so I can't speak to how long it will last. Now for the things I didn't like.

First, this is not the most comfortable headset I've ever had. The padding on top is somewhat thin and I can feel too much pressure from the band even after adjusting the length. The ear cups fit around my ears, but I've got really small ears (my father called them "shell-like"). If you have medium to largish ears, I'd skip this set. Second, you cannot use it while it's charging. You have to tilt the ear cup out to get the cord plugged into the top (see picture 3). In addition, the charging cord that came with the set is incredibly short (a bit over 8 inches). I used my three foot long cord to get it charged. Third, I tried listening to music through my cell and it sounded a little tinny to me. Now I did not play music with a lot of bass, so maybe there's some music that would kick it in a little more. Finally, the product doesn't contain a carrying case.

Will I permanently swap my earbuds for these over-ear headphones? I'm thinking probably not. The earbuds and the MP3 player both fit in a tiny case that I can put in my pocket. I may use the larger headphones to listen to books on my cell, but I rarely listen to that device in restaurants. I hope this review gave you a nice overview of these headphones.

title: Nice inexpensive over-the-ears
text:
This is a Vine Program Product Review

It has been a long time since I had a pair of over the ear cans for headphones, and these might take me back in that direction.

I'm no audiophile, but I've had various JBL speakers and headsets over the years and always found the audio quality to be good to excellent, and these do not disappoint. I found the bass deep enough for my simple tastes and range of the headphones great across a variety of musical genres. Lyrics were always clear and nothing muddled. This was true whether in noise cancelling or standard mode.

I found the noise cancelling to be quite effective. Typing on my laptop keyboard was not discernible while I had noise cancelling engaged, but turning it off I could easily pick up the clacking in the background. Even with the background noise audible, the over-the-ear seal was adequate enough that I never adjusted volume after turning off noise cancelling. My ears aren't huge, so the coverage may vary for others, but I found myself not using noise cancelling all that often. I did use it on a few flights, just to see how it impacted my flying experience, and I had no idea what I have been missing not having noise cancelling headphones before. Not having the drone of the engines in my ears for 2 hours was definitely a new experience.

First time pairing was super simple. The phones are in pairing mode out of the box on first power-up. The 2nd or 3rd or 4th time, not so much. I was quite disappointed in JBL for not having a 'subsequent pairing' instruction in their getting started guide. I have dozens of BlueTooth devices from headsets to speakers to sensors to smartwatches, and while it is always a differing experience from manufacturer to manufacturer how to get the pairing done, this could have been easier. TIP: if you're trying to pair with a second device or the phone lost pairing, you hold the volume down button while powering on until the BT light blinks and it should show up in your pairing options on the phone or tablet. There are enough buttons on the headphones that it could have been any of several combinations, so this isn't immediately obvious even for a gadget geek like myself.

One thing that surprised me was the ability for the cans to operate like a standard pair of headphones, either powered or not. This might be common in this class of headset, I'm not sure, but it was a nice surprise to see that, and it could easily come in handy if you run out of battery. Operating in a wired mode worked as well as in BT mode, though I did find myself turning up the volume a bit when in wired mode. The cable comes in the box, but it is not a standard 3.5mm to 3.5mm cable; replacement cables are easy to find for purchase if it were lost, however. The QS Guide claims it is a "detachable audio cable with remote" but there is no inline remote on the cable like many wired headsets have for controlling audio or phone calls.

For me, battery life is very good. I don't walk around all day with headphones on my head, so this is obviously something that will vary based on your use. I didn't conduct extensive and rigorous battery experience testing, but I went 5 days with sporadic usage sessions from 30 minutes to a couple of hours, normally with noise cancelling turned off, before I had to recharge the first time. On my Android 9.0 phone, the BT indicator in the notifications drawer will give you a battery charge percentage while the headphones are connected, and the light panel that shows noise cancelling and BT connection status will shift to a red light when battery gets low. I have always left charging to an overnight exercise as I do with everything else, and when charging it was always full with an overnight session. The headphones use a standard micro-USB cable to charge.

Fit of the headset was fine for me, and I found the cans comfortable on the ear, with no real stress or pinch points on my head or ears. The PLU leather covering is soft and pliable. There is a lot of adjustment play in how the cans themselves can flex against the ears as the size of the headband is changed. If you like to rest the headband on the back of your head or neck, these might not be for you, as the weight of the headband makes the cans pull down on the ear fairly significantly, so I always wore them with the headband over the top of my head. The headset is a little heavy, especially for someone more accustomed to in-ear solutions, but for me it was never uncomfortable to use them even for a long movie on my tablet. After a short time of wearing the weight disappears.

While I didn't personally wear these to work out in, I think the weight and makeup of the PLU covers on the cans wouldn't be very conducive to heavy activity and sweating. The covers don't appear replaceable so if you messed them up with sweat, you're looking for some sort of 3rd party replacement. JBL doesn't claim any level of IP rating, so this should not be surprising, but something to consider if you were looking for that.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the call capabilities and quality of the headphones. I wouldn't use something like this as my day-to-day call headset but it was very convenient and worked very well while working around the house listening to music to also be able to take a call without taking my phone out. Participants on the other end of the call had no issues hearing me and said my audio quality was very good. It was a weird experience for a person accustomed to years of Plantronics headsets attached to me ear to take a call in both ears ;-).

One thing it is taking getting used to is the number of buttons on the headset. These include volume +/-, a call control button with multiple functions, the noise cancelling button, and power. The QS Guide has a good section on which buttons do what with single or long presses (outside of the subsequent pairing function), it just takes getting used to compared to a wired headset or a phone communications-specific BT headset which only has a couple.

The only disappointing factor to me on this headset is it doesn't come with a case. At this price point that might not be a realistic expectation, but I won't travel with them again until I find one that I like. I travel too much to know what happens to electronics just bouncing around loose in my backpack, and these aren't inexpensive enough to call them 'disposable' in my view. If there were even a cheap ballistics nylon case included this would likely be a 5 star review.
