title: Very comfortable keyboard for those suffering of any sort of wrist issues
text:
I've been using ergonomic / natural keyboards for about ten years now and since the very first ones came out. This has proven to be the most comfortable one so far. I had one of these at my last job and I ended up buying one for my current job and for home.

I recommend buying the business version (this keyboard is also available in the home edition.) While a little more expensive, the business version comes with a small stand that can be removed to make the angle of the keyboard change. The home version does not come with this stand. Because of this, the angle for the home version cannot be changed and you are basically forced to use the keyboard in only two positions in opposite to four as it is the case with the business version.

People who hit the keys very strongly (as if using a typewriter), may find this keyboard not as strong. However, for someone who does hit keys very hard like me (I learned to type on a very old Remington typewriter), I have already put about three of these keyboards to the test and all the keys have survived me.

I would also definitely recommend this keyboard for anybody who is suffering from carpal tunnel syndrome or any other sort of pain around the wrist area. The support for the wrists is pretty large. I had keyboard-used tendonities and first stages of carpal tunnel and that's the reason why I had to switch to natural and ergonomic keyboards long time ago. This keyboard has definitely helped me and I'm no longer in pain when typing. Of course, everybody is different and your results may not be the same as mine. But this keyboard, along with other measures, definitely helped in my healing process.

title: Good Quality, Nice Springy Click
text:
I'm really liking this Arteck 2.4G Wireless Keyboard Ultra Slim Full Size Keyboard with Numeric Keypad, which has all the features I need, and worked straight out of the box as soon as I plugged this into my computer, using the USB/ USB-C charging cord that was included (USB into the computer, USB-C into the keyboard). I also realized that you need to move the slider button on the keyboard to "on".

This works wirelessly or wired, so you can charge while using, and the 2.4G USB receiver fob is stored in the back of the keyboard where you'd think batteries would go. The keyboard feels nicely weighted, is slim and does not feel cheap. The keys are indeed full-sized, and have pleasant indents where your fingers press. The function keys across the top, as well as the bottom row (incl. Ctrl, Fn, Win, Alt, space bar, direction keys, zero and dot) of the keyboard, are puffed up, and slightly convex by interesting contrast. The "clickiness" factor is between a mechanical keyboard and a flatter quiet keyboard, and it does have a bit of spring to each press. I don't find the clicks or the tension annoying at all, but i wouldn't be using this in bed if my husband was trying to sleep, for example.

Overall, this is a great keyboard, and i'm happy with the extra room and numerical keypad this device provides. I'd highly recommend it.

title: Not the "Magic" Keyboard but Still Good
text:
If you temper your expectations - this keyboard is just fine and, as an Apple product, is well designed. I bought it for "the daughter" along with a 2019 Ipad this past X-Mas so she could do homework. Good looking out (pats self on back), Dad.

PROS:
Connects effortlessly, via Apple's Maglock tech, to 7th generation+ Ipads.
No charging. No syncing. "It just works" immediately upon connection.
Great for writing emails or light business on your iPad. This combined with the Ipad meets the needs of my 5th grade student just fine. She uses it like a laptop to do homework.
Provides front facing protection for the iPad screen when not in use. Converts to iPad stand when in use.

CONS:
For my adult male hands, the keystrokes feel mushy and cramped.
Not optimal for intense / business use. This is a portable solution for writing long email replies and maybe doing light date entry rather than being tied to the touch screen. It does not take the place of a proper keyboard IMO. If you want to use your iPad as, essentially, a portable laptop - I would recommend the Apple bluetooth Magic Keyboard (see below).

MISC.

This is the only connective option for the standard iPad model. You can get a bluetooth magic keyboard (approx. $100 and about the same price as the Smart Keyboard) that is much nicer to type on but is a separate peripheral you will need to lug around. The smart keyboard connects directly to the ipad and, essentially, becomes one unit.

YMMV if you feel the need to dish out $300 for a connective Magic Keyboard for your ipad pro.

title: Portable, lightweight with full sized keyboard
text: This is a full sized keyboard with full sized keys. It has all the usual keys. It’s like they simply popped out the keyboard from a regular laptop or something. This keyboard is thin and ultralight. On the back it has a section that houses the batteries, nano receiver, electrical switch and wiring. This section also doubles as a lift for the back side of the top so the keyboard is angled and easier to use. The manufacturer gives you a couple batteries to start you off. There is an on/off switch on the back as well. I would prefer it to be on a side so I would not have to turn it over to turn on the keyboard. I like that there is a light on the front of the keyboard that lights up red when you turn the on/off switch to the “On” position. It turns off after 4 seconds. I also like that this keyboard has a sleep mode. It will go to sleep when you are not using it. Holding any key down for a second turns it back on. This really saves the batteries. Of course you need to turn it off if you are not going to use for a long time. The thing I don’t like so much about this keyboard is that the outer edges around the bottom are sharp. Even though they are plastic, they do not feel good on the hands or fingers. Rounded edges would be better. When you type on this keyboard the keys are not completely quiet but they are quieter than some I have used. The range from the nano receiver is about 30 feet when the batteries are new and fresh. The range will most likely depreciate as the batteries weaken. Over all this is a nice little keyboard. It is very handy for use on any device. I recommend it.

title: tiny keys, weird layout, not true multitouch (by 2020 standards)
text:
BATTERY:

the main thing i like about this is that it's rechargeable... but the battery doesn't last very long... also the chargeing cable is about 8 inches long and permanently attached to the keyboard. even though the charging cable is usb, it doesn't transmit data... so if you lose the dongle you are sol. why?

RGB:
the backlit keys are also a plus (the only other pluse). they are nice and bright but they drain the battery quickly, so leave them off, mostly. also, since they have RED GREEN, and BLUE rgbs, why couldn't they go ahead and allow you to mix the colors to get whatever color you want backlight to be? that would have been really easy..

after that it gets really bad...

TOUCHPAD:
the touchpad is advertised as multitouch with zoom, but there is no zoom. you can use 2 fingers to emulate scroll wheel, but you can't scroll left and right, the only other multitouch function is 2 finger tap == right click. that's it.

there is no pinch to zoom, no 3 finger gestures, nothing that you would expect on a modern touch interface. also, it's extremely difficult to highlight a sentence or click and drag with the touchpad.

WIRELESS:
I haven't tried using the keyboard at a distance andi didn't get it for that, so I"m not sure. it does come randomly disconnected, you can press a little button in the corner, and that fixes it sometimes, or sometimes you have to power cycle... not a big deal

TYPING:
I saved the WORST part for last.

yeah, it's a keyboard, but typing on it is as bad as it could possibly be.. Why would they make a keyboard that is so difficult to type on....?

tthe keys themselves are tiny.. maybe good if you are 8 or have small hands, but they are barely big enough for me to press them accurately. they are nice and clicky, and they register keystrokes pretty well...

UNLESS you type quickly... someone else said it tops out at about 35 words per minute... sounds about right.

probably the worst aspect of the keyboard is the right shift key is SMALLER than all the other keys and it is placed to the RIGHT of the up arrow. I actually have to lift my hand up and look at the keyboard to type a capital letter or a symbol with my left hand. it's insanely annoying and awkward...

I guess they don't really have capital letters in china, so i can see why they might have made this design choice, but when you are designing a keyboard for a certain market... you need to understand that market... PLEASE fix this in afuture revision...

using this device is a chore..

i bought it to replace a logitech keyboard that was similar, but i didn't like using AA batteries so i found this... i will probably replace it with another logitech, because that keyboard was great. or, maybe RII, please check out the logitech keyboard and see what they did right.

this could be a good keyboard with a few changes, but as it is, It's not recommended.

title: A kicky Keyboard brightens things up.  Nice change of pace!
text:
[[VIDEOID:6d7441bd4559a7ba77f6cf4452cd24dd]] Every keyboard in my house is... pretty much the same. But now.... there's a fresh breeze.

The only desktop type unit I have is my server hiding in part of the "mancave". I picked up this keyboard to brighten up that dungeon.

The KNOWSQT rounded keys remind me of the old style manual typewriters I grew up on- round keys and a bit more travel. It's not as much travel as it was then, and the effort level is the same as today's keyboards. It's a "wired" keyboard, plugs into any USB A type port, and is plug and play. I like the big red ESC key, the Green Num Lock/Caps Lock lights, and the white expanse of keys. It's not a listed feature, but I feel a bit more... creative at it than usual.

A feature I'm just loving- is that, when you press the FN button and F11 (which has a little lock icon on it), the keyboard won't accept any typed input- its "locked" until you press FN/F11 again. Any cat owner can tell you, those beasties love to type. I have pages of that stuff. Now I can preserve my documents mid-thought, or during a pause.

It will feel a bit "different" at first. But after about 10 minutes use, it was just as natural as any other keyboard. I don't have long nails- I don't think that would be a problem for most, but typing is a matter of feel. Whether using my fingertips or finger "pads" things worked well

I'd buy it again- maybe in blue next time for the nice change of scene/feel in daily life.

I have a brand new lenovo, no third party software, 2 weeks old - it's the mouse, not me.  Anyway I'm very happy with my Logitech (same company) MX Revolution that I use wirelessly for my workstation and the wired Optical Notebook Mouse I have for personal notebook use. Mouse itself is durable

Long battery life

Good mouse range

Cons:

Weak receiver construction

Receiver not integrated well into base

It’s comfortable in my hand and responds well to my touch. The only reason I need to replace it is because I often eat at my desk and sometimes that’s hard on a mouse. Also, when you consider how much time we spend using a mouse, the surface is just bound to wear down.

I probably don’t use all the features…just the wheel and left/right clicks. It rolls nicely and the battery life lasts quite a while. I like the little green light on the top to tell me it still has a charge.

I use a basic mouse pad with a built-in wrist rest and my hand and arm do not feel any strain. The rubberized grip really helps me hold onto it comfortably.

I have seen this mouse in other patterns but I stick with this dark gray version. I have a black desk and I would just prefer to keep everything monochromatic, since my office is in my home.

title: Great When New, But Fail Over Time
text:
To be honest, I'm really tired of these mice failing.

They work great at first, then eventually quit scrolling or, worse, get stuck in scroll mode and drive the cursor to the bottom of the page for no reason. Two have failed on me. The first was purchased in 2011 for $36, the second in 2014 for $30. Both failed to scroll reliably and made using them impossible. Other, cheaper, wireless mice work better, or at least longer.

This mouse has nice features like left/right scrolling by tilting the scroll wheel and they work on many different surfaces, but those features fall by the wayside if the thing doesn't work at all after some time.

I've tried blowing it out with compressed air to clear debris, but it didn't fix it. Haven't come to taking it apart and cleaning it, as some proffer, because it's simply not worth the time.

For how much these mice cost -- $66 for the two -- they should be bulletproof. Better to buy cheaper wireless mice and throw them away when the fail.

I'm trying the $11 [[ASIN:B074DV98R7 VicTsing 2.4G Wireless Mouse Wireless Optical Laptop Mouse with USB Nano Receiver, 6 Buttons,5 Adjustable DPI Levels,15 Months Battery Life]] next. I could have purchased six of them for what I've put into Logitech MX Anywhere mice, both of which become landfill fodder.

Logitech has lost my Anywhere MX mouse business.

title: Defective from the factory
text:
Logitech used to be the by far best peripheral equipment for computers. I loved their stuff! When you bought a Logitech keyboard or mouse you knew it would perform flawlessly and last for a long time. Sadly this is no longer true. Logitech's quality has deteriorated hugely in the past couple of years.
I bought two of these high priced mice because they are perfect size for a traveler like me and both mice after about six months or so developed button issues and scroll wheel issues. Buttons would no longer function and the scroll wheel became unbalanced so that on hyper scroll it would at the end of the scroll try to roll so the unbalanced part of the wheel would be on the bottom scrolling your page up and down in front of you. After a loooong warranty process that took me two weeks of daily emails with Logitech "customer service" (not really a service but more a pain in the neck) back and forth, they finally sent me a brand new MX mouse as a replacement. Guess what. The new mouse was defective right from the factory out of the brand new box with the same scroll wheel issue. I give up. Actually my cheap M505 mouse performs decently so far but this high priced mouse is of inferior quality. Be warned! I'd stay clear of this mouse! So sad to see Logitech go this way.

title: In addition to Windows, it works in varying degrees on Android and Chromebook
text:
This is a handy little bluetooth mouse. If you are pressed for space, this is indeed a space saver. For example, if you have a laptop with a touchpad, you need some elbow space to use the touchpad or use an external traditional USB mouse. With this tiny one and touch scrolling, you can just move your finger up and down and left and right the mouse surface.

Despite the small size, it was surprisingly usable, even during some long sessions with a desktop computer. Obviously it can't replace a desktop mouse for power users, especially if you are used to mice, but it is good enough to get things done without getting in the way if that's the only mouse you have with you. It worked on various surfaces.

This is a really small mouse. It is roughly 5.5cm long, 6cm wide and its height ranges from around 1cm to 3cm at its highest. With the battery installed the mouse weighs 2.2 ounces. There are two buttons at the bottom, one is a mechanical slider button that slides the battery door open and the other is a press-me-please button that turns the mouse on and off. A longer press on that button (after you turn on the mouse) sends the mouse into pairing mode. At the bottom of the mouse, in between those two buttons, there is also a blue light (the bluetrack light).

When you turn on the mouse, a green light turns on briefly on the tall side of the mouse and then turns off. The blue light at the bottom of the mouse also turns on. To turn it off, a simple press of the power button at the bottom of the mouse is enough and you can easily tell it is turned off because the blue light turns off.

To enter pairing mode, first turn on the mouse, and then long press the power button until you see flashing lights on the tall side of the mouse. Pairing mode is also party mode, with the light on the front side of the mouse alternately flashing in red and green and the light at the bottom of the mouse flashing blue in between the red and green flashes on the tall side of the mouse. Then follow the instructions on your device to complete the pairing.

On Windows 7, the computer needed rebooting after installing the Microsoft software that Windows decided it needed. I was able to connect and use the Wedge mouse without problems using a 99c USB bluetooth dongle.

The mouse also worked on Android and Chromebook but obviously it does not have the luxury of dedicated Microsoft device drivers that the Windows versions do.

On a Google Chromebook (the $250 Samsung), it works fine but you don't get all the features. Touch scroll works but you can't scroll by pressing the mouse button and moving the mouse up or down. Touch scroll can be a bit jumpy on secondary touch scrolls. It is fine when you scroll to a place in a page, but when you scroll for a subsequent time, the new scrolling position is not always the one you expected it to be (higher or lower). Maybe it's the way I am using it or I haven't been able to adjust for the Chromebook, but I haven't had this issue with Windows. On the plus side with Chromebook, you do get the context-sensitive sub-menu (eg open in new window, etc) with a long press.

On Android, things vary depending on which device and which browser or apps you use. On a 10-inch Acer tablet with Honeycomb era hardware (Tegra 2) running Acer's version of 4.0, it works okay but not as smooth as Windows.

With the Google LG Nexus 4, it is a pretty good combo in landscape mode if you use apps that could benefit from a mouse with touch-scroll. You can also use it together with a bluetooth keyboard. However, there is an issue with using it together with Wifi. After you connect the mouse, Wifi data stops flowing. As soon as you disconnect the mouse, Wifi data flows again. I suspect this is not the mouse's fault, because this happens with some other (but not all) bluetooth devices and the LG Nexus 4 with the current software (late March 2013) has a variety of Bluetooth related issues when you google around. Hope is not lost however, because the mouse does not affect cellular data, that continues to flow regardless.

One issue to note with web browsers on Android. All the major ones work with the button-press-and-move-mouse scrolling (finger-equivalent). However, the current version of Firefox (late March 2013) does not work with touch-scroll. Touch-scroll worked with the other Android browsers I tried (Chrome, Dolphin, Opera). Touch-scrolling on Android with Tegra 3 is smoother than the Chromebook.

The mouse comes in a squarish box in the typical Microsoft hardware box colors (red, white, gray) but unlike those ugly keyboard boxes, it looks nice enough if you want to give this as a gift. The box is 15cm by 14cm and 5.5cm tall. Measurements approximate and rounded. The box opens as if this was a watch or jewelry with the mouse front and center. Under the mouse compartment you will find the brief user guide in four languages (English, Spanish, Portugese, French), along with the Limited Warranty and legalese Product Guide.

The mouse needs one AA battery to operate. One AA alkaline single use battery is included in the box. I did not try rechargeable batteries with it.

The original price when it came out was rather high, but as of late March 2013, it is more reasonable (around forty). The original price made it a bit of a luxury for geeks but the price at review time is a lot more reasonable.

title: Oustanding for Windows 10, tablet style computers
text:
Like it or not, the Windows Start menu is no more. Thus, the right mouse button is now king in Windows 8 and 10, where adding/sorting the main screen is absolutely essential.

Unfortunately - and for tablet style computers akin to my ASUS Transformer - the trackpad is mediocre, at best. Right clicking becomes a chore, where accidental clicks/swipes create navigation chaos.

The Microsoft Wedge Touch Mouse is the panacea. Small enough to travel anywhere, ridiculously responsive, easy on/off, and a swipe function that works like a dream. The wedge shape likewise puts a traditional mouse to shame. It takes the pressure of wrists, as the fingers now run the show (based on angle). It feels really well made for something only $25 (at time of purchase).

Finally - and perhaps most importantly - this mouse paired instantly with Windows 10.

title: What I was looking for!
text:
To give you a bit of background, I'm using this mouse, and it's matching keyboard [[ASIN:B008OEHPKM Microsoft Wedge Mobile Keyboard (U6R-00001)]] with a Windows 8 desktop computer that I built. I've been in IT for 14 years, and am VERY picky about my mice and keyboards, and I was hesitant to buy these items site unseen. Lucky for me, I ended up making a good choice.

First off, I HATE clutter, so the size was important to me. I realize that this mouse was built for mobile users, and a lot of expert reviews will tell you this mouse is not for every day use, but for me the smaller the better. Both the mouse and keyboard fit comfortably on my keyboard tray, and I have room to spare. Keep in mind, this mouse is TINY. My fiancé's flash drive is actually longer than the mouse is tall. If you can get around the small size, this mouse is quite functional, especially when paired with the Windows 8 Mouse and Keyboard Center. With it, you have the ability to program application specific functions to the mouse button's but I haven't found a practical use for this feature...yet. You can even identify what, if any, programs have trouble scrolling using the touch gestures, adjust scroll speed, enable/disable flick gestures, etc.

The single finger scrolling works well, as do the flick gestures. I hold the mouse between my thumb and ring finger to avoid having any issues with gestures, etc. I find the mouse to be very responsive, and have had no issues using it over the last week. You can see that Microsoft paid attention to the build quality, which you would expect given the price of this item.

The only thing I really miss is a back button on the side of the mouse to use with web browsing. At times, I find myself hunting for it with my thumb.

Most of you will want to think hard before buying this mouse. It's definitely not for everyone. It's a great addition to a tablet (Windows 8 or otherwise) due to it's small size. For use in a situation like mine, you'd want to give it more thought. If at all possible, see the mouse in the store, or make sure you understand the return policy of the vendor you're buying it from. It's TINY...and it won't be for everyone.

For those of you who take the time to adjust to it, and really give it a shot, I think you'll be satisfied with your purchase.

title: It's a mouse, it works.
text:
When purchasing a bluetooth mouse, or any bluetooth device, an important factor is how well it connects and how well it STAYS connected. After all this time, the industry still can’t make up its mind about how bluetooth works:
- Microsoft with their mouse and Sony with their controller that pair without the need of a code (which Android’s bluetooth stack doesn’t support).
- Mice and keyboards that will not reconnect after it wakes from sleep mode.
- To this day, bluetooth devices still can’t wake a computer from suspend state.
So when I get a simple bluetooth mouse for a good price, and it actually works as expected, I was happy.

For my review, I’m comparing the Bornd mouse to the [[ASIN:B006428K7I Motorola 89519N Bluetooth Mouse]] which I got in a set that included the [[ASIN:B004L9MBH6 Motorola Wireless Keyboard for Motorola ATRIX and XOOM (Motorola Retail Packaging)]].

With the Motorola mouse, its frequency somehow conflicts with the Motorola keyboard, resulting in sticky keys, as in “I’m having a good daaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay”. Conversely, the keyboard interferes with the mouse where the computer would actually lose connection with the mouse for a few seconds after typing, or lose connection completely.

What I liked about the Bornd:
- Pairing was simple using the button at the bottom of the mouse.
- Operating distance is about 5 feet, but this may be because of my computer’s bluetooth antenna
- Takes a single AA battery which lasts over a month of moderate use (2 hours per day)
- Mouse movement is good. No need to adjust mouse speed in the control panel.
- Accuracy is good. Editing images using Pixlr.com, I’m able to select precisely the parts of the image I need.

What gave me trouble with the Bornd:
- When you first put your hand on this mouse, you will not feel that it is very well built. The plastic is completely smooth and the mouse wheel seems to rattle when you shake it. I got used to it after a few minutes, though.
- The mouse reconnects with the computer most of the time, but sometimes it was necessary to turn the mouse off and on again after the computer reboots or if the computer was out of range for an extended period of time.
- Lately, I’ve been experiencing double-clicks when I click on the left mouse button once. I’m usually able to fix this by getting angry and slamming the mouse down a couple of times. This may indicate a build quality issue with this mouse.

In my specific case, the Bournd did not interfere with my Motorola keyboard at all and it seems the sticky key occurs only when the batteries on the keyboard runs low.

title: Close, but no Anker.
text:
My company bought this mouse for me, but I still wanted to review it here. Here's what's up: I have a large women's hand at 8" around the knuckles. I usually wear a Medium men's glove or Large/XL women's, so compare from there.

I have a wired Anker vertical mouse at home. I wanted a wireless Anker mouse for work, would have gone with the wired version... but the website the company uses does not offer Anker. This is the most similar design offered, so that's what I ordered and here it is.

The box came with the USB chip and the mouse and a set of batteries. No instructions required. Put batteries in mouse, switch to "on" (on the underside), plug in the USB and do mousey things. Turn it off when you go home from work for the night, and the batteries will last much longer. I haven't done a glass test - honestly I have no idea why people are so bothered by whether a mouse will work on glass - but I'm using a fiberboard clipboard as a "mousepad" and it's working great.

Now for the things you care about:

- BUTTONS: the left and right click buttons and scroll wheel are awesome. That's where it ends. The "next page" button sits squarely on my thumb pad, so I could use that if I ever had an occasion to do so. I have to kink my thumb back to hit the "page back" button so I will definitely never use that one. I don't know what the DPI button does, but that's at the top and easily accessible.

- MATERIAL: this is one shiny mouse. It's very slick plastic. It's going to scratch like crazy when I drop it. It's lightweight, which concerns me about the durability. I guess I will have to re-visit this review in a while to let you know how it's holding up.

- RF CONNECTION: seems effortless and strong. There aren't a ton of RF things in my office to interfere with the mouse. The USB is plugged into the right side of my computer and I of course use the mouse on the right. There is about 30" between the mouse and receiver. I mostly have the mouse pointing away from the receiver with no issue.

text:

The Logitech software will give you a low battery warning, but by the time you get it the mouse is about to die. Even on the Bluetooth menu, you do not see battery percentage. A couple of minutes of charging will give you an hour of battery, so the battery drawbacks are not dire.

Other than that, it is very good. Scrolling is not quite as smooth as with magic mouse, but close. The size is a huge advantage, great for traveling. Clicking does not require nearly as much force as on Apple's Magic Mouse.

NOTE: Mac users must install the Logitech drivers, or the mouse will be difficult to use for scrolling. The Logitech preference panel is LAME -- a panel with a single button that launches a standalone app called Logitech Options.

Overall I like it but wish that I could at least see a battery percentage indicator on the menu bar. I have two, one is always charged up for when the other dies.

title: Has a Mind of It's Own
text: I have been using this mouse for about three months and just ordered Logitech's MX's Master from Amazon to replace it.  I thought it was kind of elegant looking and had fairly good reviews and was cheaper than the Apple Magic Mouse 2 but similar enough to justify the purchases but I have not been happy with it for the following reasons.  It is very small and so not particularly comfortable and feels awkward to use.  "The straw that broke the camel's back" was the inadvertent and unexpected activation of the zoom function when scrolling and the occasional unexplained loss of the scroll function.  These two problems, which were annoying and time consuming to compensate for when working, was too much.  So, I will no longer use the Mouse on my home computer.  It probably will be OK to use with my laptop when on a trip.  I would not recommend it for regular use and certainly not for work related or time related functions.

title: It's an upgrade from my beloved M510's.. But not by much
text:
I just want to give a shout out to the Logitech M510.. That mouse is solid as a rock, I've been rocking those mice for several years now but have been wanting to upgrade for some time since mice have come a long way.. Honestly, the M510 is still perfectly fine even in 2020.

Let me start with the feel, I don't have particularly large hands. They're pretty average I'd say.. With that being said, this is a pretty small mouse and definitely does take some getting used to. I've owned it for a little over a month now and I'm honestly still not 100% comfortable with it, but I'm starting to get there.. If you have large hands I would completely skip this mouse, you will not be comfortable at all.

The buttons are a bit sensitive which also takes getting used to, I have found myself miss-clicking many times because of how much more sensitive and how little response it takes for it to register a click. This definitely takes some getting used to.

The accuracy of the mouse is very good and it tracks very nicely. I purchased a M720 before this mouse because I read all the great reviews of that mouse. But it tracks like garbage, whereas the MX Anywhere 2s tracks really well. Definitely a bit better than my old M510 in this regard.

Battery life: So far it's been great. I don't use Bluetooth though which might have an impact. After my first charge I have yet to charge it again and it's been over a month. According to the Logitech app I have 2/3 battery life bars remaining and it shows "good".. It'd be nice to have a more solid battery percentage. I do appreciate that it has a rechargeable battery, though USB-C would've been nice..

Now on to bad..

Dongle & Connectivity: I have a love-hate relationship on this next topic.. The dongle, I love that they reduced the size of it! It's about time! The dongle is now almost half the size of the old one.. There's a catch though... The new dongle has HORRIBLE RANGE!! I Cannot go more than about 3 feet from the laptop before the mouse starts experiencing connectivity issues. My laptop has Bluetooth, but I prefer to use the dongle since it preserves battery life and it has less delay.. But I may have to move to BT if this gets annoying enough.

My second biggest annoyance is the middle click button.. It is no longer on the scroll wheel.. Instead pushing down on the scroll wheel activates the infinite scroll feature which is nice.. But I rarely ever use that feature. The middle click button is now about 1cm or so behind the scroll wheel. Which you wouldn't think is such a big deal. But it's really hard to get used to and it completely breaks up your flow when you're using the mouse and have to use the middle click often.

With these issues I cannot say that the $50 price that I paid vs the $35 I spent on my M510's (Bought one in 2017 for $15 & one in 2016 for $20) is a good buy.

It's a nice mouse, but it definitely has a learning curve and it's definitely not without it's faults. Try before you buy.

title: The perfect living room or presentation mouse.
text:
Updated, 6/4/2021
So, since I've purchased this thing, I've paired it with an iPad, two different Samsung tablets, 3 different desktops, a laptop, and a Steam Link.

I can say without a doubt this is probably the most versatile mouse I've ever used. The center-click button does take some getting used to, and no on-the-fly DPI adjustments, but it's more than precise enough for graphic design / modeling work, and my daughter and I have used the heck out of it for gaming. Still use it daily for modeling and managing 3D printing software. This thing has been dropped a zillion times and even got dunked in the toilet once. (Don't worry, sanitized it with bleach)

It's still going strong and still has amazing battery life.

I've probably owned a hundred or so mice from Razor, Logitech, Corsair, and even Apple mice. Not to mention a myriad of other brands here and there. I go through about 1 mouse every 6 to 12 months because of my rampant computer usage.

This mouse, has outlasted more than a dozen others, and still performs.
I'm buying another. Not because I need a replacement, because the original is still going strong. I just want another because I have 3 desktops a laptop 2 tablets and a steam link, and the mouse only has 3 pairing slots. That's really the only downside.

Most people don't have as much tech as I... so it's perfect for the 99%.

All of that being said, for FPS gaming, probably not the best in the world if you like sniping and switching DPI settings on the fly.

However there are ways around the lack of hardware buttons. There are ways to hotkey DPI / sensitivity settings, so an easily overcome snag.

This is a fairly rugged travel mouse as well. I've flown with it multiple times and driven across the country with it. Still going strong. Switch it off, toss it in the backpack, live your life.

Yeah, great mouse.

title: Tops if you are Right Handed
text:
I have always liked the Logitech mice, keyboards and web cameras. I wanted to try out the multi system capability of this mouse. I have a small Logitech Bluetooth keyboard (K380) that supports multiple systems. This mouse is sold as the "Logitech Pro Mouse", but is really the same as the "Logitech M720 Triathalon" a Multi-Device Wireless Mouse – Easily Move Text, Images and Files Between 3 Windows and Apple Mac Computers Paired with Bluetooth or USB, Hyper-Fast Scrolling, Black. Perhaps I was not reading the description correctly, but my assumption was that the USB dongle that came with the mouse was Bluetooth. It comes with the USB 2.4 GHz unified receiver.I found this out after a short call to Logitech tech support that was very helpful and did not require me to be on hold for what usually seems like hours. 5 Stars for Logitech Support.

The mouse worked fine with the unified receiver out of the box. I was wanting to use it Bluetooth however so I ordered an inexpensive Bluetooth receiver for my older desktop from Amazon and it was delivered the next day. It was the ZEXMTE Bluetooth USB Adapter CSR 4.0 USB Dongle Bluetooth Receiver Transfer Wireless Adapter for Laptop PC Support Windows 10/8/7/Vista/XP,Mouse and Keyboard,Headset. (It worked great out of the box as well.

I as then able to get the Logitech mouse (M720) and keyboard (K380) hooked up and working. I've not experimented with the Unified Features yet, but have attached the devices to my iPhone and a laptop system.

Cons: I'm left handed and it can be difficult at times to manage the M720 mouse. I do have a Logitech M510 that is more ambidextrous in shape and handling I keep with my laptop. I wish that there was an M720 in a shell similar to that of the M510. Perhaps there is a DIY project in the future.

title: Too big for small hands
text:
Like most of us, I spend a lot of time working on the computer. I’m also picky about mice, but am trying to be as ergonomic as possible in my peripheral choices, to prevent problems down the road. My current daily driver mouse is Logitech’s MX Master 3 and I use a palm grip.

I’ve wanted to try a vertical mouse since reading about them, but for me, the DELUX Vertical Mouse won’t be the one. The mouse is just too big for my small hand. To give an idea of my hand size, I wear a size small women’s glove.

My hand doesn’t fit naturally on the mouse. My whole hand slides down the body, so I have to keep tension in my hand and arm to keep my fingers in the proper place to be able to use the mouse buttons. It’s not comfortable; my hand and wrist hurt within minutes. My thumb keeps sliding to sit on the bottom of the side buttons, so it’s fortunate for me the side buttons don’t work on Macs.

I tried the mouse with and without the palm rest, there was no difference.

On the plus side, the mouse charges via USB-C, and can connect via Bluetooth or wireless. If you don’t use it, the wireless dongle fits neatly into the base of the mouse without impeding using it.

title: Disappointed... created pressure on wrist
text:
Was looking forward to this mouse. Construction and scrolling feel very very premium. Clicking buttons have way too much travel to activate, but, most importantly, with or without the wrist extension, it sits too high to be comfortable.

Pairing can be done with up to three devices: Two via bluetooth and the third one via its USB-A dongle. Connecting to different devices was effortless.

Compared to other ergonomic mice, this one is more vertical and taller. As a result, the user's hand is more in a vertical position, causing pressure on the outer side of the wrist. This happens with or without the wrist extension.

With the wrist extension, moving the mouse involves moving the entire forearm. This would be great if I had to immobilize my wrist for whatever reason. But not great to draw with the mouse or for finer gestures.

The charging port on the mouse is USB-C, but the radio dongle is USB-A. That makes sense because the majority of USB-C computers don't have enough ports and docks/hubs don't typically have USB-C data ports.

As I said, construction and overall feel of the mouse is good, but it simply sits too far off the table to be comfortable.

Overall I think this mouse works perfectly well for what I need, there is gonna be some lag with a wireless mouse no matter what but I haven't noticed anything really and so the fact I didnt spend more is a great plus for me.

I am not running dungeons in WoW anymore due to my RA so whether this mouse may or may not live up to that sort of experience I can't say, but I probably would just use my corded to be safe.

I have used it to remote play games like Minecraft, Monster Hunter World, Resident Evil, Ffxiv, and various smaller games like Stardew Valley or platformers. The mouse worked great, I didnt notice any lag or anything!

Another super plus is I like being able to sqitch between using it for my laptop and PC without having to switch the dongle out, I just have bluetooth set for the laptop and the dongle for my pc, makes remote playing extra easy and extra lazy ..so score!

title: It's your hand as much as it is the mouse
text:
OK. I have a wrist and arm problem which is actually a neck problem. I'm having surgery soon but its effects will be limited.

So, I've tried all the ergonomic mice including the much-vaulted Evoluent Vertical Mouse D. It's a great mouse that is built like a tank, but it does not work for me. And that's the point. A mouse that one person loves may not be loved by all. It's a personal fit thing so quality is not the only factor.

This Penguin mouse is by far the best for me. Some people say it doesn't feel like a quality mouse but I don't get that read from it. It seems well built to me.
So:
Pros:
"Joystick" shape is best for me since it does not require "sideways" pushing to click.
Buttons are firm enough that I can feel the switches click. I've lost some feeling in my fingers.
Ambidextrous switching via a button low in front.

Cons:
DPI switch is on the bottom. Fast switching is impossible. In the next version, put that button on the very top, guys.
The Base...Oh My, what a huge base. This is the worst feature of this mouse. It's so wide that it is hard to slide, even on a superior quality mouse pad, and will bump into the keyboard and side monitor. This huge base is not necessary and desperately needs to be reduced in size. Next model cut it down about three-fourths of an inch on the sides and back but do nothing in front. The designers probably thought it would fall over without this huge base but even if it does when not being used it won't when you are holding it.
The charging cable is proprietary. Needs to be USB C in the future.

Final Notes: Description mentions Bluetooth Functionality. There is none. You need the included USB Dongle to make it visible to your OS. Also, it needs to weigh a bit more.

I recommend it if it looks interesting to you. I'm happy with mine but look forward to the next model to see what they do with it. I'll be checking their website occasionally to see if there's anything new.

title: Basic, colorful, reasonably priced mouse for someone who needs nothing more than this
text:
Love the color and design of this mouse. It comes with one battery already inserted and it is as easy as plugging the tiny wireless receiver into a USB port, having the system automatically set it up, then turning it on. The mouse is responsive, has a center wheel, and the typical left and right buttons. This is a reasonably-priced (cheap) basic mouse because I do not need all the bells and whistle and I do not do gaming.

Be aware that the "c" in the M325c means that the receiver is NOT a unifying receiver. This means only the mouse will work with this receiver and I cannot pair a keyboard with it without plugging in another wireless receiver into another USB port. If it had the star logo on the receiver, I would be able to pair a keyboard with that one receiver. I put a link to an article about this difference in the comments section of my review for those who are interested.

title: Great wireless ergonomic mouse!
text:
This mouse has been a lifesaver as far as my wrist goes when working. It has a very comfortable form factor. A lot of vertical mice are "too vertical." They stand so upright that it is awkward to use them in combination with your horizontal keyboard. This wireless mouse is vertical but has a slight tilt inward so that it is not too hard to get used to and use. The butons have a silent but noticable click.

The thumb area of the mouse has a place to rest your thunb inside of a circle that has controls and an LED light. There is a forward and backward button on the left and right side of the circle, and a DPI button to adjust the mouse speed on the top of the circle. The bottom of the circle is the button for changing color effects on the LED ring on the mouse.

The mouse has 5 built-in DPI settings that you can adjust the mouse speed with. In addition, the mouse connects to up to 3 different devices (1 with 2.4 Ghz dongle, 2 with Bluetooth). This means you can use the same device with multiple computers. There is driver software that you can download from the manufacturer website, but it tends to only open when you are using the dongle connection. If you have the mouse connected via Bluetooth the software will not recognize the mouse connected. That is the only real negative to this mouse.

I am very satisfied with this mouse. It has been the best ergonomic wireless mouse I have owned, and the cost is very low. There is no reason not to try this mouse out. Once you get the hang of how it works, and you feel how comfortable it works, it will quickly become your go-to mouse for working on the computer.

title: Ah, lovely.
text:
Like I imagine many people have done here, I wanted a very quiet clicking mouse. But I also wanted a mouse that isn't portable or compact--just a regular mouse like the one that came with your office PC. (In the picture, the Rapoo is on the left, the other two are mice we've likely all seen/used before.)

And on that note, wired. Not wireless. Wireless just means the toddler runs away with it. No, thank you.

And that's exactly what you're getting here. Classic mouse shape, classic mouse feel.

Except one big difference, very little click click click click.

The sound is similar to if you press a key on your keyboard as softly as possible until it finally depresses. That light thud noise of the membrane collapsing. It's extremely quiet, but does give a nice tactile click to your finger.

And if you're like me, just wanting to play a little solitaire or what have you while the wife sleeps, or even at the office when you're clicking away on your PC (Yep, I bought two), this mouse is a welcome break from the endless clicking.

In short, I love it. If it doesn't hold up, I'll update the review. Out of the box it's great. Cord is less than 3mm OD, considering there are 4 cables inside, I'm guessing they're the absolute thinnest wire gauge that can support 100 mA continuously, AWG 31. Because you know, quality!

Includes some paper card with a promise of a free gift "Free Rapoo Product" if you visit their website (which gets flagged as unsafe by your browser) to "active your warranty", enter some personal information as well as your Amazon order ID and agree to submit a review.

Yeeeeah I'm not doing any of that. This is a direct from Shenzhen product and I can just about guarantee you're not getting jack monkey squat if you actually proceed with this super dodgy offer.

But I'll gladly supply a review anyway. But really people, don't do this.

So all in all? Eh, seems okay. Wire is obviously sub par, but the mouse seems to work well. I have a spare fabric cord from an old mouse, I might take this one apart and solder on a new cord. If there's a weakpoint in this mouse, it's this shrimpy cord.

title: Nice and quiet
text:
Nice, quiet mouse at a great price. It's on the smaller size, just what I needed for carrying in the computer bag. I have long fingers, but not necessarily large hands, and this fits perfectly for me. The scroll wheel is nice and smooth (and also quiet). You can feel some tactile "knurling" when you scroll, so it's not baby's-butt-smooth, but it's not like scrolling over a circular-saw blade either.

Using the USB dongle, the mouse is very responsive. The Bluetooth connection seemed a little laggy to me. No stars off unless it does the same when I test it on another PC.

I do not intend to install the Logitech Options software so I cannot speak to the usefulness of Flow or reassigning buttons.

Pros
- USB and Bluetooth connectivity
- Can use with up to two devices.
- 7 buttons: L, R, Center, Center-Left, Center-Right, Back, Forward. Eight if you include the PC selector button.
- Very quiet left/right click buttons
- Nearly quiet center click and back/forward buttons
- Uses one AA battery (preferred over non-replaceable battery)
- Battery life advertised at 2 years.
- Has an on/off switch on the bottom

Cons
- Possible laggy response using Bluetooth. I need to test on another PC to be sure.

Other consideration:
- The USB dongle storage is behind the battery door. If you frequently remove the dongle from the PC, this might be a concern for you (it's not a problem for me).

Setting it up was super easy and since I already had a logitech dongle for my work keyboard plugged in I just connected it to that. On my laptop I have it connected via bluetooth. The smooth transition between the two devices of the mouse pointer is almost indistinguishable as though my laptop was a third monitor on my work desktop. There is a slight hiccup as it goes from one to the other but very acceptable. One of the main selling points to me was the additional buttons on the mouse for forward and back. Saves me so much time.

Also as with most Logitech mice, the device works smoothly on just about any surface. Mousepads be damned. As a matter of fact, it seems to work worse with a mouse pad. My only complaint and I am well aware that this is a nitpick, is that the click of the buttons is a bit loud. I can understand how it can annoy some people. But overall this mouse at $30 is a friggin steal.

UPDATE: 8 months later and I am STILL using the generic battery that came with the mouse. The power consumption on this thing is phenomenal and please keep in mind that I use the mouse all day at work and then I take it home and use it a little bit at home in the evening and on the weekend. Point being is that the mouse is not being used once a week.

title: Ergonomic but moves pressure point to side of wrist.
text:
This being the first time I have used an ergonomic mouse I had certain expectations regarding how it would solve the problem I usually have with mice. While it removes the pressure points from the center of the wrist the tilt move that point to the bone on the side of your wrist. This is easily cured by a cushioned mouse pad. So why then use it if you still need a soft spot for your wrist? Ease of use! The mouse has a variable sensitivity rate that is nice and high for us power users (move the mouse a fraction and you can span the entire screen), or dial back the sensitivity for doing very fine and slow cursor movements. The two buttons on the side are excellent as the back and forward buttons. I have become an active user of the back button. Saves having to move the mouse to the screen icon to go back.
The Bluetooth connection works about 90% of the time. When you walk away for a bit, or don't move the mouse for a while it goes to sleep. Which requires you to hit a button to make it wake back up. On my Linux environment that translates to a few seconds of time wasted on movements and button play to get Linux to realize the mouse is in play. Using the USB adapter for 2.5Gz communications, there is no waiting for anything to wake up. It simply works. Downside: it eats another port on your computer. If you have limited ports but also have Bluetooth, your best bet is to keep it on Bluetooth.
Overall I have enjoyed its speed and button options. Work very well for what I do. Takes a little getting used to but you'll be a pro in a short amount of time.

=================

It takes a AA battery, and occupies one of two USB ports on the laptop. There's a slot inside where you can put the USB connection when you're not using it. There's no power switch, so take out the battery if you don't want it to be drained.

I'm not crazy about the shape of this thing. The boxy shape doesn't fit naturally into my hand and it feels weird. I prefer a more traditional shape, but it's not like it's stopping me or anything. It's not hard to click or scroll and it doesn't make my hand tired. Overall, this gets the job done and doesn't look bad doing it. Four stars.

Although, to be fair, it does make it hard to determine if the thing is powered on or not!
At first I loved it, the scroll wheel is good, even the modes to control the dpi were a pleasure to cycle through. But then it got... jumpy. Like, sometimes I would move the mouse and it would feel like it paused and had to catch up all of the sudden. Movements didn't seem to mimic mine in real time. I do a lot of video editing and have to shuffle clips around with precise movements, I found this inconsistent behavior really unsettling to work with and needed to go back to me old boring flat mouse. If you don't have a mouse or just want to make browsing easier on a chromebook or something like that, it's good in a pinch, especially for the price. But sadly it is not reliable enough for moderate to heavy users in my opinion.

title: Quiet and super fast Bluetooth setup - no Emoji function with iPadOS
text: Within a minute of taking this out of the box, I had it paired with my iPad. It was seriously so easy to just pair and go, and I love how it can be paired with three different things (just push a little button on the bottom of the mouse to switch between computers/iPads). It feels okay in my hand - not the highest quality I’ve seen (plastic is very basic and it is pretty lightweight as well), but it doesn’t feel cheap. The color is so fun, which is the main reason I got it. Also it is very quiet and doesn’t have any loud clicking. The one thing to mention is that the circle button under the scrolling wheel doesn’t have any functionality with an iPad. Nothing was happening when I kept clicking it to try and use the emoji shortcut, so after heading over to Logitech’s website i saw “*Emojis and software are currently supported on Windows® and macOS only.” So maybe iPadOS will eventually support this capability, but as of now it is useless. Overall I still like the mouse a lot for it’s ease of use, quietness, and color.

title: Is it silly to like a cute mouse?
text: I got this mouse for two reasons: it's a Logitech which is my favorite brand of mouse, and it's pink. I like that it's bluetooth as well as wireless, and it's easy to connect. Works right out of the box. Fits my hand well, smooth as glass operation, all the things I expect from a Logitech. I have only one small quibble, and unfortunately it turned out to be an issue. The cover is held in place by magnets. Not bad usually, but I dropped the mouse hours after acquiring it--I know, I know, clumsy of me--and the cover popped off. No one's fault but my own. But the left-hand button now requires me to push harder than I did before, which is a distraction when I'm using it. I can't swear the lid popping off caused the problem, but I would prefer that the lid was attached more securely, as it provides added protection to what's under it. Anyway, just a thought. Still love the mouse...

title: Pretty In Rose, Quiet & Responsive, Customize For Mac & Windows, Easy Bluetooth Pairing-Feels Small
text:
This Logitech Pop Mouse is stylish in rose, contemporary and lightweight. I feel like this mouse isn’t ideal in terms of ergonomics for me, mostly because it’s small and raised in a way that I don’t feel like my hand gets enough support and my hand hangs over the bottom awkwardly. It’s okay for short intervals but not a mouse I’ll use for longer periods. For reference, I wear a women’s size L or XL in Isotoner gloves, size M in disposable vinyl gloves and size L in nitrile gloves. The size and style of the Pop Mouse seem better suited to a teen or others with small hands.

This mouse is quiet, fast and responsive. It can be customized using the Logitech software compatible with Windows 10 and Mac OS 10.15, 11 and 12. The software does not work with iOS, so the emoji shortcut feature won’t work with iPad. It was impressive, however, how quickly the mouse Bluetooth paired with my iPad mini 5 (iOS 15.2). And it works well at the same time as my Bluetooth paired Logitech MX Mini keyboard. The inability to use the emoji shortcut on iPad is a nonissue for me as my keyboard has a dedicated emoji key, but it may matter to some. While not ideal for me due to size, this is a good portable mouse for casual use by those with smaller hands. 4 stars.

title: Good but wanted more features
text:
I bought this in a time crunch. My wired mouse was getting hard to use because the scroll wheel had shifted out of place. I had several wireless mice around, but none of them still had their wireless receiver. And they were before the days of Bluetooth. So, I had was in the market for a new one.

This one is nice. It fits the hand well and all. But, I realized that it did not have the features that I was used to. First, it is not a quiet mouse. I did not notice at first, but when it penetrated my fog of concentration, I could not unhear it. Click. Click. Click! And, this was not great for conference calls either.

The other issue was that it tracked slower than I would like. I was still using my wired mouse at this point, so I did not want to change mouse settings via software. I really missed having a dpi button on my mouse. This is important to me as I use a laptop on an extended display to a 2nd monitor. So, I need to be able to zip from one end of the screen the other - quick enough to unmute and answer a question during a conference call.

Have to click to wake up the mouse kept catching my attention - which means it was on it's way to annoying me... I have worked with computers for so long, it's like an extension of me. It needs to be intuitive to use and not interrupt my flow.

And, at this point, I figured out that I would need to use two different computers at once. And, while I could pair this wireless mouse with a wired one, the USB ports required were a challenge. My newer computer has no USB C ports at all. So, this limited my set-up options. Secondly, I now had 2 mice crowding limited desk space.

So, I learned that there was such a thing as multi-device mice. And, I found one that can switch between two computers and a iPad - with a simple LED indicator so that you know which device you are controlling. I bought the also designed to be silent and to switch between different dpi. All these features and it was only $3 more.

This is what I bought to replace this one - Arteck Multi-Device Wireless Bluetooth Mouse with Nano USB Receiver Ergonomic Right Hand Silent Clicking for Computer Desktop PC Laptop Mac iPad and Windows 10/8 iPad OS Build in Rechargeable Battery

So, to sum it up, I would say that I need the speed and responsiveness of a gamer's mouse with the silent clicks and 3 device connects like an office worker. So, this mouse is ok. But, if you are an advance or intense user, you may find that it does meet your needs.
